Maybe you want something bold and full of personality like the iconic Rockefeller tree in New York City. Perhaps you’re looking to go classic with a full lighting system included or something to match your favorite wreaths. No matter your preference, there’s a good chance that once you go faux, you’re never going back to the real deal. After all, there’s no watering involved, cleanup is a breeze, and easy storage is usually part of the design.

Our list below includes pre-lit trees that take the guesswork out of nostalgic spruces and even an enticing winter white design. And to really achieve a professional-looking holiday home, we’ve tapped experts like Kendall Jenner’s holiday floral designer Jeff Leatham and AD-darling designer Shea McGee for exclusive tips on how to level up any faux tree.

Reviewer: Divya Viswanathan, VP, commerce portfolio lead

This big, beautiful tree is inspired by the Fraser Fir. Known for its rich, dark green coloring and full silhouette, this tree is native to the Appalachian Mountains and has the distinction of being the type of tree most often used as the official White House Christmas tree.

To be honest, we can’t tell the difference between Balsam Hill’s faux version and the real thing. BH's impressive “true needle” foliage features 40 variations of branch types throughout and the effect is incredibly realistic.

The tree is available just about any height and light variation you could want, all of which feature an easy plug system. Easy plug trees have all the light strands plugged into the center pole, so all you have to do is place the three sections together and plug the tree into an outlet. There’s no need to ever unplug or take off any light strands.

The style pictured above is “color + clear,” which allows you to switch between multicolored lights and white lights via remote. For pre-lit trees with a single lighting style, there is an attached foot pedal to turn the lights on and off. The Twinkly light style features built-in app-controlled smart lights from Twinkly.

This beauty looks like it was plucked right off the tree farm, but all you have to do is just pull it out of the box. Speaking of, let your tree breathe for a day or two after you take it out of the box. That way, the branches can fluff up on their own before you decorate the tree. The tree features hinged branches, making setup and teardown straightforward (just push each hinge down and pop into a storage bag). If you’re looking for a large tree, and a full tree but don’t want to spend a fortune, this is a good, solid pick from The National Tree Company. The National Tree Company has been making holiday trees and decorations for more than 60 years, and they have plenty more styles to choose from on Amazon and Wayfair.

Reviewer: Stewart Savin, senior SEO analyst

Like a real-life Douglas Fir, this faux tree is designed to have a darker hue than other evergreens. Its needles are also longer and flatter than other evergreen varieties, growing out on either side of each branch rather than all the way around it.

Reviewer: Pujah Shah, global director of audience development, analytics & social

King of Christmas is a holiday-focused brand in the business of memory-making, with a vast inventory of artificial trees, garlands, and decorations to get your home in the Christmas spirit. The brand provides helpful written guides on assembling, shaping, and storing your tree, as well as video tutorials for a more visual learning experience. King of Christmas also donates thousands of trees to underprivileged families and communities impacted by natural disasters each year. The brand’s pre-lit Alpine Fir, a species native to Washington state, feels like spending the holidays in the Pacific Northwest, and allows you to enjoy festive vibes minus the maintenance. While pricing leans on the higher end, each faux tree is handcrafted to mirror the distinct shape, color, and growth pattern of real branches.

Another one of the prettiest pre-lit Christmas trees is this Blue Spruce. The full foliage on this fake tree includes realistic needles in blue-green and silvery hues paired with light brown stems, just like an authentic Blue Spruce. Like all Balsam Hill trees, it comes with an off-season storage bag, protective gloves to use while shaping the tree branches, and extra bulbs.

Reviewer: Brie Schwartz, commerce director Glamour

Another tried and true, super affordable option straight from Amazon. We appreciate our contributor Brie Schwartz’s approach to the fake tree game. Instead of spending big bucks going for a super realistic tree, she aims for over-the-top flocking and lots of lights to lean into the fact that she prefers the faux variety (and to have her tree up for as long as humanly possible for the season). Go big or go home, right? If Schwartz’s approach rings true to you, too, this might be the perfect tree for your household.

Reviewer: Kate McGregor, commerce market editor

We’ve turned to Quince time and time again for their high quality, yet affordable bedding and soft goods over the years. This artificial spruce is the newest addition to our catalog of tested items from the brand. (Fun fact: It’s even the main image of this story in case you were wondering which faux tree made it as our model this year). Quince’s take on a spruce employs an interesting branch design: The back end of each limb features bushier evergreen bunches while the front-portion presents tips that look more realistic. This clever system actually makes the tree look more lush from within while still maintaining the appearance of something life-like on the surface. Commerce market editor Kate McGregor noted in her review that the tree did give off a fuller look, and was especially handsome once decked out with a merrily maximalist slate of ornaments from some of our favorite holiday hubs like John Derian and Anthropologie. Just be mindful that the more realistic branch segments can leave a semi-sticky residue on your hands (an issue you’d have with real tree too, we might add).

Reviewer: Lauren Arzbaecher, commerce producer

Let us set expectations here: For a tree that’s under $100, you are probably not going to find the highest quality option for your Christmas tree. That said, we wanted to put one to the test to see how it held up in person. If you are looking to prioritize price over super realism, we think this option makes a lot of sense.

Reviewer: Stewart Savin, Senior commerce SEO analyst

Unconventional tree colors—like gold, silver, or white—are smart options if your taste favors a non-traditional Christmas tree. It brings all the drama but doesn’t pretend to be something it’s not. This all-white Kingswood fir tree won’t dampen any pastel-forward design schemes in the way something with a more authentic evergreen look might. Plus, the snow-like white needles provide a neutral canvas for making your ornaments stand out. Tester Stewart Savin liked that the slim design of her seven foot-tall selection can fit into more narrow crevices, though it’s available in seven-and-a-half, nine, and 12-foot options with wider diameters. A disciple of Kathy Hilton’s design philosophy—that every room deserves a unique tree set up during the holiday season—Savin plans on keeping the Dunhill Fir from the Holiday Isle she tested last year as her main tree, and this smaller silhouette with “winter wonderland vibes” in her bedroom or sunroom.

How easy was it to assemble your tree (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? Given that artificial trees are, by their very nature, annoying, I’ll give this an 8 overall. The [storage] bag it arrives in is a little awkwardly wrapped, and the entire set is kind of heavy, but it’s a really intuitive assembly process and could easily be done by one person. The pieces snap in place with very little effort. The big time suck is fluffing up the needles and zhuzhing the branches until it looks full. The entire process from bag to completely assembled took about 10 minutes.

What was the quality of the tree packaging? Will you be able to store your tree for future years? The bag is a little flimsy, but that’s my only gripe. It fits well and isn’t too bulky to stow in the small basement storage unit in my New York apartment. I imagine I’ll easily be able to store the tree for its entire lifespan.

How long did it take to fluff and prepare your tree? Did you see a lot of needle loss in the process? It took about five minutes of fluffing to get the tree to look real. The branches were pretty flexible and held their shape well. No needle loss at all!

Did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? N/A

Did your tree live up to your expectations and was the size accurate? The sizing is accurate and perfect for my apartment; there was just enough room for a star at the top. I expected it to look a little lackluster, considering the price and the fact that the shredded plastic “needles” at the core did look cheap. The “trunk” also left something to be desired; it had that same shredded plastic, and the brown metal base starts pretty abruptly and kind of high up. But the branches transitioned to realistic needles at the right point, and I was really impressed with the look—it was almost exactly like the real Fraser firs I grew up with. I’d recommend it to anyone who wants a medium-sized, realistic-enough artificial tree without spending a gazillion dollars.

How full is the tree (scale of 1-10, with 10 being the fullest)? It’s about a 6 or 7, which is perfect for my needs. I grew up with sparser trees, and I like having enough room to decorate.

How realistic is the tree? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most realistic)? Let’s go ahead and say 8! Fully decorated (and maybe with a spruce-scented candle going), it passes for the real thing and doesn’t make me feel sad about having a hunk of plastic in my living room. We also set this up as a prop for a holiday party at a bar and we overheard someone say, “And they even got a real tree!”

Who says faux trees can’t be nostalgic? This unassuming Norwegian Spruce with an under-$500 price tag impressed contributor and discerning holiday decorator Jake Smith in multitudes. Fluffed up, Smith notes that the tree is on the sparser side, but that just means more room for decorations. “The branches transitioned to realistic needles at the right point, and I was really impressed with the look—it was almost exactly like the real Fraser firs I grew up with,” he says. The tree even went on the road with Smith who used it as a centerpiece for a holiday party hosted at a Brooklyn bar, even overhearing someone say, “And they even got a real tree!” Recommending it to anyone who wants a medium-sized, realistic-enough artificial tree that’s not overly expensive, Smith tells us that “fully decorated (and maybe with a spruce-scented candle going), it passes for the real thing and doesn’t make me feel sad about having a hunk of plastic in my living room.”

Reviewer: Alyssa Marino Williams, AD Senior Video Producer

How easy was it to assemble your tree (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? This tree was very easy to assemble, taking around 30 seconds, so I’d rate it a 10. The lights are already embedded into the branches and they’re separated into two parts—tags on the wires indicate which wires connect with each other and which should be plugged into the wall, but it’s also pretty self explanatory.

What was the quality of the tree packaging? Will you be able to store your tree for future years? Everything was packaged well—I appreciated how compactly the tree fits into its box. I’ll plan to store the tree in its original packaging during the off season: The cardboard box that housed all the pieces, and the base that was stored in a bag within the box (zero styrofoam—a plus by my account).

How long did it take to fluff and prepare your tree? Did you see a lot of needle loss in the process? I lost maybe 30 or so needles in the process, the fluffing took a few minutes and at its fullest, the tree didn't get as filled out as I had hoped, but that’s what ornaments are for.

Did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? This prelit tree is very easy to install—so a 1 in terms of difficulty. The lights were already attached to the branches, and as I mentioned, the two segments just needed to be attached to each other before planting the assembled tree into the base. The two batches then just needed to be connected to one another and then plugged it into the wall. There were also tags on both sections that indicated which light set should go directly into the wall and which should be plugged into the other set.

Did your tree live up to your expectations and was the size accurate? This tree is perfectly sized to fit smaller spaces—its petite stature would make any corner look more festive. I plan to use the full-size Dunhill Fir in my main living room, and this tree elsewhere around my house. Perhaps in the primary bedroom or sunroom, but the verdict is still out!

How full is the tree (scale of 1-10, with 10 being the fullest)? On a fullness scale, I'd rate the tree an 8! I plan to fill the gaps with an assortment of ornaments and more lights.

How realistic is the tree? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most realistic)? I’d rate this tree a 2/10 as far as how realistic it looks—it’s fairly obvious it’s not a real tree. I think for the price and the size it’s a fantastic value. It’s very festive, easy to install, and immediately puts the holiday spirit in the room.

Petite trees guarantee that even the most unassuming corners can be full-out festive during the holiday season. With its tiny stature, tester Alyssa Marino Williams appreciates that this spruce look-alike is easy to assemble and very portable, making it a cinch to move into rooms that needed more cheer. “[Tree setup takes] around 30 seconds,” she says. Instead of tangly string lights, the prelit option includes bulbs embedded into the branches that emit an elegant, even glow throughout the fake foliage. And as experts like Kendall Jenner’s holiday floral designer Jeff Leatham tell us, “Always, always, always go for pre-lit.” Fully fluffed, the branches weren’t as robust as Marino Williams hoped they would be, but fortunately that’s where decorations come in. “I plan to fill the gaps with an assortment of ornaments and more lights,” she says.

Reviewer: Pujah Shah, global director of audience development, analytics & social

How easy was it to assemble your tree (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? 10,000/10. This is hands down one of the easiest artificial trees I’ve ever assembled. It comes in roughly four or five sections that simply stack on top of one another, and that’s pretty much it! No complicated instructions or wrestling with branches, and best of all, no untangling lights. The whole process felt almost too easy for a nine-foot tree.

What was the quality of the tree packaging? Will you be able to store your tree for future years? The tree arrived quickly and was thoughtfully packaged, with each section clearly labeled and easy-to-follow instructions that made assembly a breeze. Everything felt well organized from the moment I opened the box. Since the tree comes apart in just a few sections, I expect storing it for future holidays will be relatively simple. Given its size, though, I’ll probably invest in a dedicated storage bag rather than attempt to fit everything back into the original cardboard box.

How long did it take to fluff and prepare your tree? Did you see a lot of needle loss in the process? About 30 minutes, tops! The branches practically fall into place on their own, so most of that time was spent making a few adjustments to get everything looking full and even. Compared to other artificial trees I've owned, it required surprisingly little effort. And the shedding was almost nonexistent. I barely noticed any needles falling off, which was another welcome surprise.

Did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? Again, this tree gets a 10,000/10. The tree comes with 3,400 tiny, pre-installed LED lights, and they all illuminated as soon as the tree was connected. No plugging individual sections together, no hunting for missing connections, and absolutely no stringing lights—it was instant Christmas magic. The lights also have multiple settings, including a gorgeous twinkling effect, and can be controlled through a remote or the Hubspace app.

Did your tree live up to your expectations and was the size accurate? Absolutely! At nine feet tall, it's a substantial tree and makes a beautiful statement in our foyer. The silhouette is elegant, and the sheer number of twinkling lights gives it a really lovely, festive glow. What really won me over, though, was how little effort it took to get there. I do think some other artificial trees I've owned have more convincing foliage, but the overall effect here is still gorgeous. The combination of its size, shape, and all those lights makes it a lovely centerpiece for the holidays.

How full is the tree (scale of 1-10, with 10 being the fullest)? 9/10. It’s a beautifully full tree with a classic, symmetrical shape that looks impressive even before adding ornaments. There are a few areas where you can see slightly farther into the branches, but overall, it has a lovely, lush silhouette without requiring hours of fluffing.

How realistic is the tree? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most realistic)? 7/10. It's definitely a beautiful artificial tree, but I wouldn't say it's the most realistic one I've owned. Up close, it’s fairly easy to tell the branches are faux, especially compared with some higher-end trees I've had in the past. That said, its overall shape is lovely, and once it's illuminated, the effect is pretty spectacular. I'd say this tree prioritizes ease, fullness, and a little holiday sparkle over perfectly imitating a real fir.

Home Depot’s Grand Duchess Christmas tree is internet famous for a reason. The TikTok-viral holiday decor favorite first gained traction a few years ago; creators found the tree’s easy setup and realistic appearance provide an impressive canvas for both minimal decorations as well as ornament-maxxing. The micro fairy LED lights are equipped with 10 settings that allow you to switch between elegant white lighting schemas and fun multicolor displays.

How easy was it to assemble your tree (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? 10—compared to the fake tree my family had when I was young, which was a tedious mess of individual branches, this was a dream. It only took around one minute to put the pieces together.

What was the quality of the tree packaging? Will you be able to store your tree for future years? The tree arrived in a plain old cardboard box with a plastic handle. Nothing fancy but definitely reusable.

How long did it take to fluff and prepare your tree? Did you see a lot of needle loss in the process? Fluffing and spreading took a few minutes, but it was pretty easy. The branches are easy to shape and adjust. There was absolutely no needle loss whatsoever.

Did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? 10 for sure, I can safely say this was the easiest lighting job for a tree ever since the vintage-style, C7 multicolor LED lights are wired into the trunk of the tree.

Did your tree live up to your expectations and was the size accurate? Size-wise, this tree is as big as I hoped it would be—around five feet, since the ceiling in my living room is criminally low. I grew up with fake trees (my dad is allergic to pine) and I can’t state enough how easy this was to put together. (Maybe we just had a really fussy tree? I haven’t been keeping up with all the advancements in fake tree technology.) All just to say, I like the tree. I appreciated that I didn’t have to deal with any cords, and since the lights are wired through the trunk, all I needed to do was plug the top half into the bottom for the entire thing to light up. I was worried that these would be the LED lights that have that annoying visual buzz, but the old-school vintage bulbs were perfect.

How full is the tree (scale of 1-10, with 10 being the fullest)? 6/7, there’s some open space between the branches, but I don’t need my tree to be an impenetrable cone of green. This design leaves room for plenty of ornaments and swags of garland, in a way that I feel is visually balanced.

How realistic is the tree? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most realistic)? 6: The exterior branch ends are a more realistic-looking material, while the interior branches—mainly there it seems to fill out volume—are obviously fake. You can’t tell unless you’re really up in the tree’s business, so it doesn’t bother me. I imagine that for a more expensive tree, each branch might commit to the same degree of realism, but if it means saving a couple hundred dollars, I’d say it’s worth it.

The Holiday Living collection from Lowe’s is giving Home Depot’s Grand Duchess a run for the internet’s favorite tree this year, with a full range of artificial trees that have been praised for their unique lighting schemes. One of the most distinctive from the line is this design, whose branches are adorned with vintage-looking multicolor LED light bulbs, with several festive speculators heralding it as a nostalgic “throwback.” Tester Wilder Davies noted that the tree had impressively no needle loss while he was setting up. And while there’s some open space between the branches, our tester didn’t need his tree to be an impenetrable cone of green. “This design leaves room for plenty of ornaments and swags of garland, in a way that I feel is visually balanced.”

Did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? 7—This tree is pre-lit with LED lights that are controlled with an included remote. As this was my first time having a pre-lit tree, it took me a second to sort out how the lights connected. I’m used to putting on lights myself, where the strands connect at the ends into one long extended strand. Rather than the top section of the lights connecting to the middle, then the middle connecting to the bottom, the lights on this tree each have a power cord that connects to a splitter at the bottom level, which then feeds a single cord to the outlet. That means you have to wind the cords through the branches for them to reach the splitter, which made it a bit less straightforward than just plugging the tree in and it being all set.

Did your tree live up to your expectations and was the size accurate? Because I am just two inches shy of six feet tall, it makes gauging height fairly easy—standing next to this tree I can confidently say that the size is accurate. With a relatively simple setup and a fairly convincing look, this tree met my expectations. It may have even converted me to a pre-lit devotee. I wasn’t sure if I’d like the LEDs at first, but the glow is gentle enough for the cozy look I want out of my holiday decor. Plus, not having to budget an extra 20 minutes for wrapping strands of lights around the tree for a decorating process that is already pretty time consuming was delightful.

I would still say there’s some gaps that require a bit heavier hand when it comes to decorating to make this tree appear super full.

How realistic is the tree? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most realistic)? 7—As someone who grew up in a real tree only household, I’m not sure any artificial tree will completely fool me, but this one does a serviceable job. It’s full enough to feel cozy, and the texture and shape of the branches mirror the real thing nicely. The two places I think it would be more convincing are the needles and overall color. It may have even converted me to a pre-lit devotee.”

Puleo International is another well-known name in the artificial tree game, selling at outlets like Amazon, Wayfair, Home Depot, and Lowe's. The brand’s slim Fraser fir was exactly what tester Emma Tubbs was after: “I wanted a slimmer tree so I wouldn’t have to rearrange my living room too much, and this was the perfect width,” she says. The tree’s versatile look and approachable price point also helped it overtake the Best Choice Products Pencil Christmas Tree for our ‘Best Slim Tree’ pick. “The 7.5-foot height is perfect for my tall ceiling, and the tree is slim but still full and realistic-looking so it doesn’t look gangly,” says Tubbs.

We always research products thoroughly before including them, and test every single one. Our reviews are thorough, in-depth, and honest. We put ourselves in the shoes of the shopper (because most of the time, we are the ones shopping!), and make sure that we’re answering the questions that we would want answered in the buying process.

We favored natural-looking trees that are easy to set up. We also took shipping into account and tested trees that arrive not only in style, but with speed.

All trees that were reviewed were unboxed, set up (and lit up) by our contributors. They lived with trees and experienced all they had to offer firsthand, so that they could share the real deal with our readers.

What Size Christmas Tree Is Right for Me?

First and foremost, the height of your fake Christmas tree should depend on the height of your ceiling. A good rule of thumb is to keep your tree at least one-and-a-half feet lower than your ceiling, otherwise, it will look crowded. “I like to leave about six to12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in,” says Shea McGee (more on the designer’s holiday advice below). Both McGee and Jeff Leatham, the floral designer who helped mastermind Kendall Jenner’s festive holiday house, agree that seven to eight feet hits a sweet spot in most homes. “The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe,” says McGee.

Some people want to avoid the hassle (and extra cost) of buying a fresh tree each year, while others are allergic to real trees or are concerned about the fire safety hazard that comes along with real trees (they can become highly flammable as they dry out). Others (including people with pets) know that a real Christmas tree can be bait for disaster. Fresh or faux is really a matter of personal preference, and anyone who wants a fake Christmas tree should go for it. Leatham points out that in faux trees, the branches don’t drop, the coloring stays vibrant, and there’s often more structure to add extra ornaments.

Is It Better to Get a Pre-Lit Tree Or to Do It Yourself?

Choosing if you want your tree pre-lit is one of the first decisions you’ll make when navigating the vast artificial tree world. Pre-lit options are the preference of holiday decor gurus like Leatham. “Always, always, always go for prelit—it makes the tree look more full and realistic,” he tells us. Our editors like that pre-lit Christmas trees are convenient to set up (opposed to blindly garlanding string lights) and how they help guarantee your lighting scheme will look uniform. That said, drawbacks include potentially difficult repairs. While you can easily unstring removable lights to troubleshoot, built-in LEDs might pose bigger technical issues. On the other hand, stringing your own lights may be a more complex, time-consuming process, but you’ll ultimately have more control over which areas of your tree are spotlighted.

How Should You Decorate Your Christmas Tree?

You’ve gotten your tree up, fluffed the branches, and poured yourself a nice cup of hot cocoa or eggnog to celebrate—now comes the fun part: decorating. While there’s no right way to decorate your Christmas tree, we looked through our archives for some tips and tricks to give your setup some extra sparkle.

If your mentality is “more is more,” your holiday hero will be Kathy Hilton, who greeted AD back in 2021 with four artificial Christmas trees decked out with all the bells and whistles (emphasis on the bells). One tip we’d steal from Hilton is the idea that the decorations don’t have to go up all at once. “I normally start decorating in October, then keep adding until December,” says Hilton.

Kendall Jenner, on the other hand, favors a more traditional tree, dipped in nostalgic classics like tinsel, twinkle lights, and vintage Christopher Radko ornaments that were passed down by her mother, Kris. Her designer reveals that she even loves stringing popcorn for the tree and dried orange slices on garlands. “Every year, more and more of my clients want more traditional holiday decorations that they can invest in, collect, and pass on to other generations,” says Leatham. “I love that idea of seeing the same ornaments every year and having them bring back wonderful memories.” Since we have a feeling you have your own collection of heirloom Christmas decorations that have been collecting dust, we’d look to the supermodel for inspiration.

Color scheming your ornament display is one way to set yourself apart from the pack. “Red and green are traditional Christmas colors, but I love to break away from tradition and use bright jewel tones to create a dramatic and sophisticated look for the holiday season,” says Annie Sloan, color expert and creator of Chalk Paint. Stylist Dorcia Kelley of Kelle Miles Studio also suggests using a planter instead of a traditional tree stand or skirt for a modern look. “When hanging ornaments, you want to make sure you’re hanging it towards the end of the branch instead of right at the tip. This way, they’ll be more stable,” she says.

We also recommend playing with shapes, textures, and finishes to create as much interest as possible. AD’s perfect Christmas tree (pictured at the top of this article) features lots of vintage-inspired John Derian ornaments that bring on the kitsch, accented with classic ball ornaments in a range of sizes to create depth and dimension. A color palette of muted blue and bold metallic hues complement the deep green branches while slivers of silver tinsel add holiday pizzazz.

Fluffing your artificial Christmas tree is the key to convincingly faking the real thing. Most of the time, your tree will arrive with all the branches up-turned straight out of the box, and you’ll first want to mount the tree in its stand or collar. Next comes the actual fluffing—as reviewer Pujah Shah mentioned, it’s a smart idea to wear some work gloves to avoid any pricking that might occur while you’re working through the branches. Starting at the bottom, you’ll fan the largest branches down, layer by layer, until you reach the very top (where the branches become much shorter). If your branches have smaller tips built in, we like the center-right-left method of starting toward the base of the tree and positioning the smaller tips first center, next towards the right, and lastly towards the left, until you’ve reached the end. After that, you’ll go branch by branch, noticing that your tree looks full and much more lush with each adjustment. Afterwards, all that’s left to do is make any minor fixes to eliminate bald spots and voila!

What’s the Best Real Christmas Tree to Buy?

Again, that’s completely a matter of personal preference. Trees come in a variety of hues, some with a dark green, some with a blue tint, and others with a bright shade. Some have spiky needles while others are soft to the touch. Trees vary by geographical region and what's native to your area, but some of the most popular options used as Christmas trees across the U.S. include the Fraser Fir, Balsam Fir, Douglas Fir, and Blue Spruce (all of which are available in faux varieties, as well!).

How Does the Lifetime Cost of a Faux Tree Compare to Annually Buying a Real Tree?

While how much your real Christmas tree costs will vary depending on its size as well as where you live in the United States, expect to spend anywhere from $40 to well over $100. In a few years, that running total will start to cost you, but with an artificial tree, you’ll pay the total cost up front. High-quality trees can also last you up to 15 years, making the sometimes extravagant price tags more digestible, especially in the later years when you’re no longer burdened with figuring out the logistics of strapping that netted Douglas Fir onto the car roof.

Flocking refers to the process of dusting your artificial Christmas tree with a powdery white overcoat to mimic the appearance of fresh snowfall. Some trees—like the Yaheetech tree Brie Schwartz tested—come pre-flocked, but if you prefer a DIY moment, ready-to-flock sprays are also available at most big box retailers. We like Balsam Hill’s guide to flocking your tree, which details a recipe for homemade flocking, as well as all the safety precautions you’ll want to take: Like wearing protective gear, flocking in a well-ventilated environment, and ensuring you’re using non-hazardous materials. (Though if your budget allows, we think it might be best to invest in one of the brand’s ready-flocked trees.)

In the grand scheme of artificial Christmas trees, King of Christmas and Balsam Hill are widely known as the crème de la crème, thanks to their realistic appearance, convenient setup, and thoughtful extras like complimentary storage bags for the off-season. While both fall into the category of more luxuriously-priced holiday decor, Balsam Hill’s price points are slightly higher ($349 to $4,000+ while King of Christmas ranges from $229 to $3,000+).

In our own quests for the most elite faux trees, we’ve also tried both brands. Commerce vice president Divya Viswanathan called Balsam Hill’s Fraser Fir “the Christmas tree of my dreams,” while contributor Andrea Lewis previously called her Blue Spruce from the brand “a lovely addition to our holiday traditions—elegant, easy to manage, and captures that cozy, Christmas air perfectly.” AD’s global director of audience development Pujah Shah became a King of Christmas convert last holiday after testing the brand’s Alpine Fir tree. “I wanted something tall, sleek, and a little bit dramatic that felt intentional in a modern space but still cozy enough for family chaos—it nails both,” says Shah. We think that both brands are great options—it’s hard to beat how realistic Balsam Hills designs are, and holiday floral designer and one of our experts, Jeff Leatham even named King of Christmas as his favorite brand. To choose the right brand for you, we recommend figuring out what will suit your space and your decorations, as well as establishing a price point you’re comfortable with.

We tapped the designer and creative force behind one of our favorite interior brands, McGee & Co., on the best ways to make your artificial Christmas tree really pop this season. Read on for her advice on how to make merry with a beautiful, yet intentional holiday set up.

Is There Such a Thing as an Ideal Sized Christmas Tree?

“When you’re choosing a tree, the ideal size really depends on your space. I like to leave about 6–12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in. For most standard spaces, a 7-7.5-foot tree hits the sweet spot. If you have tall ceilings, you can absolutely go bigger—9-12 feet fills the volume beautifully. And in smaller rooms, a slimmer silhouette keeps things festive without overwhelming the layout. The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe.”

What are Some of the Design Benefits of Choosing an Artificial Christmas Tree Versus a Real One?

“I love the flexibility an artificial tree gives you. You know exactly what shape and fullness you’re getting, and the branches stay right where you want them—which makes decorating so much easier and more polished. They also hold up all season long, which is great if you like to decorate early. And of course, you can reuse them year after year, which means you can invest in the style you love and bring it back every holiday.”

How Do You Make an Artificial Christmas Tree Look More Realistic?

“Start with a tree that already has a natural, realistic base—good branch texture goes a long way. From there, keep your palette cohesive so the whole tree feels curated instead of busy. I love layering garlands because they add that organic movement you see in real trees. Then finish with meaningful ornaments, ribbon, and a few organic touches—like dried citrus or pinecones. Those add warmth and authenticity, making even a faux tree feel beautifully lifelike.”

“Both options have their place. A pre-lit tree is all about ease—the lights are perfectly placed, and you get that warm glow the minute you plug it in. It’s great if you want a beautiful tree without the extra steps. An unlit tree gives you more creative freedom. You can layer different styles of lights, change the mood from year to year, and really customize the look. It takes a bit more time, but it can feel incredibly intentional. So, if you want quick and polished, go pre-lit. If you love the process of styling every detail, unlit is the way to go.”

The easiest way to make your artificial Christmas tree look like a real tree is to, well, cover it up. Go heavier on the decorations this year: Think garland, Christmas lights, pinecones, ornaments, a tree topper, etc. We're talking the works. Check out our go-to holiday decor tips that will make the best Christmas trees look even more magical.

It’s affordable in bulk, doubles as a garland, and covers quite a bit of real estate from low to high. And who doesn’t love a bow? We pulled an option to satisfy the minimalists as well as some embellished trim that’s got major maximalist appeal.

A dead giveaway—no pun intended—that your tree’s a fake is the base: that plastic, mechanical-esque tree stand. Cover that metal stand up with a festive tree skirt (or basket!) as you would with real Christmas trees.

If your tree doesn’t have pre-strung lights, head to the holiday aisle for some white or multicolored lights. Some of our favorites include unconventional and more delicate-looking lights that don’t necessarily scream “Christmas.” They’ll draw the eye to the center of the tree and take the attention off of the branches. Besides, you can never have too many lights in your home decor during the holiday season.

When scouting out ornaments for your tree, look for options with serious heirloom potential. Kendall Jenner’s Christopher Radko’s classic ornament collection is a good example—and Etsy sellers have troves of vintage ornaments to start your own traditions or recreate the supermodel’s holiday style. These miniature bulbs we found at Terrain are a fun way to create more depth when paired with larger balls, and we like that the different colors really pop when your tree is lit. We also turned to John Derian for gorgeous, traditional options pictured on our tree.

#4705. Netflix’s The Altruists Tells a Compelling Story of Love, Money, and Fraud. Here’s What Really Happened.

The true story behind Sam Bankman-Fried, Caroline Ellison, and the $8 billion crypto collapse is even messier than the show lets on.

NETFLIX’S LATEST HEADLINE-MAKING limited series The Altruists has a lot of big names attached to it. There are Irish and American actors Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner, respectively, playing up their dorkiest selves to portray Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison. (Ostensibly while Garner desperately awaits casting in a possible Madonna biopic that has been in development hell for what feels like forever.)

Who, you ask? Well, if you’ve avoided the cryptocurrency market and carbon-positive NFT gorillas in the past several years, we can’t really blame you. But what you need to know is that Bankman-Fried and Ellison were the heads of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX as well as lovers. FTX, and the love between them, notoriously collapsed when Bankman-Fried was arrested and accused of stealing over $8 billion in customer funds.

Why is this story about fraud (of which Bankman-Fried was eventually convicted) called The Altruists? Ironically, FTX was purportedly created as a company that gave away as much as it earned, based on the principle of effective altruism—words that got everyone in the finance world hot and heavy with excitement. Until news came out that Bankman-Fried and other FTX executives had spent billion-dollar-sized wads of cash “on luxury hotel stays, private planes, DoorDash orders, trips to Jimmy Buffett's Margaritaville, and, in the case of one top executive, a $2.5 million yacht,” Business Insider reports. FTX was also known for hosting an ultra-luxe conference in the Bahamas that featured famous folks including Bill Clinton, Tom Brady, and the musicians Steve Aoki and the late Liam Payne of One Direction, who in 2024 fell to his death from a hotel balcony in Argentina at the age of 31.

So, yeah, we’re dealing with a twisted and extremely millennial story full of curveballs and screwballs. But whether you’re watching The Altruists or simply hearing about it, what do you need to know about the true FTX story at the heart of it? We’ve got you covered below.

The Altruists is as much a love story as it is a story of financial doom: The two were intertwined with Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, who met at an investment firm and fell in love. Bankman-Fried would found FTX as well as its sister cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research, while Ellison was CEO of Alameda Research, which funneled money from FTX.

FTX was on an upward trajectory in the early 2020s, garnering Bankman-Fried the nickname of “Crypto King.” The company, once worth $32 billion, nosedived into bankruptcy in 2022 while also being investigated by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Justice Department. Bankman-Fried “sounded surprisingly calm” in an interview with The New York Times amid FTX’s freefall. “You would’ve thought that I’d be getting no sleep right now, and instead I’m getting some,” he told the publication. “It could be worse.”

Yes. In fact, things could and did get a lot worse for this once seemingly altruistic finance dude. He and Ellison broke off their romantic relationship amid FTX’s collapse in 2022. (“She wanted more from it than I was able to give,” Bankman-Fried testified, according to the Wall Street Journal. To which one can only wonder: More than $8 billion?)

On March 28, 2024, Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and was additionally ordered to “pay $11 billion in forfeiture for his orchestration of multiple fraudulent schemes,” the Justice Department announced.

In total, he was convicted of two counts of wire fraud, two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering.

What’s curious is that his right-hand woman, Ellison, only got less than two years in prison for her part in the cryptocurrency fraud, though she did plead guilty to two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit commodities fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. She was also ordered to forfeit $11 billion.

Her relatively light sentence can be explained by the fact that, though the “very math-y” Stanford graduate helped orchestrate the multibillion-dollar scheme alongside Bankman-Fried, she became a star witness for the prosecution against her former boyfriend. The prosecutors offered her a sweetened deal to shorten her prison time in exchange for cooperation, information, and testimony.

She testified, NPR reports, that as Alameda found itself in a financial hole, Bankman-Fried directed her to take more money from FTX customers to bail the company out. “We were in a bad situation,” she said.

U.S. Attorney Damian Williams said of Bankman-Fried’s scheme that it was “one of the largest financial frauds in history, stealing over $8 billion of his customers’ money.”

Their love may be over, and they are both convicted felons, all of which gets packed into the final episode of the eight-part The Altruists. But at least Ellison is moving on. Sort of. After being imprisoned for less than two years, she is now a free woman.

In September, Ellison formally joined Manifund “to develop our funding platform and research how to effectively direct philanthropic dollars,” the company’s CEO Austin Chen announced, per Oxygen. She had reportedly joined the nonprofit funding platform and philanthropic organization on a trial basis at first and went by the innocent-sounding pseudonym “Carol.” This work is in line with her stated belief in effective altruism, which in turn became a multibillion-dollar con, which doesn’t sound all that altruistic or effective.

“On FTX itself, I remain conflicted. It was their money and spirit that enabled the Future Fund, and I still admire many aspects of FTX and the individuals who worked there,” Chen wrote. “But also: FTX did wrong. Its collapse harmed users (myself included), and damaged the movement which I deeply care about.”

Chen is a big believer in redemption. “I’d like to give her the opportunity to contribute back to the world,” he wrote. “I hope that the world will concur.” Which is very generous of him. Maybe she’ll even get a Nathan Fielder-hosted documentary one day.

Bankman-Fried, meanwhile? He’s still behind bars on that 25-year sentence. Thankfully for him, however, he is incarcerated at the low-security California federal prison Federal Correctional Institution Lompoc, which is known for its open dormitory and room-type housing.

Maybe he will find a new way to be altruistic. Or, at least, stop committing federal crimes.

Even if you pride yourself on eating whole foods and cooking healthy meals, it can still be super hard to get all of the vitamins and minerals your body needs. Plus, your nutrient needs change as you age.

For instance, “as women navigate through the wonderful world of the menopause transition, there are changes, health-wise, that happen,” says Leslie Bonci, RD, a sports dietitian based in Pittsburgh. As your hormone levels start to decrease, you may be more likely to lose bone density and muscle mass. When these changes happen, “there are certain nutrients that are going to be needed more than others,” she adds. That’s when it can be helpful to turn to a supplement.

Meet the experts: Leslie Bonci, RD, is a sports dietitian based in Pittsburgh. Navya Mysore, MD, is a primary care physician, women's health expert, and WH advisory board member based in New York City.

Knowing which supplements you should take in each stage of life may be complicated, but we found the right experts to simplify everything. Consider this your supplement roadmap.

First, have a conversation with your primary care physician—they should know about all of the medications and supplements you’re currently taking or are considering. Your doc will help you ensure supplementation is the best course of action after considering your holistic health care plan. Then, they can rule out any potential medication interactions and decide which dosage is best, says Navya Mysore, MD, a primary care physician, women's health expert, and WH advisory board member based in New York City.

Here are some of the most common interactions, per Dr. Mysore and Bonci:

You also might want to get blood work done before starting a supplement, especially if you think you may have a deficiency. “Checking things like iron stores (ferritin), vitamin D, or B12 can tell you if you actually need a supplement and how much,” says Dr. Mysore. However, you don’t need blood work if you’re just taking a basic prenatal or multivitamin.

Just remember: “Supplements are a complement to—not a replacement for—eating,” Bonci says. They’re just one piece of the puzzle; in order to live your healthiest, longest, best life, you’ll want to make sure you’re eating nutritiously and exercising consistently.

Sorry to our gummy lovers out there: “Capsules usually win—they tend to absorb better and have fewer fillers,” says Dr. Mysore. “Tablets are fine but a bit more variable.” Unfortunately, gummies are often underdosed and may not include key nutrients like iron, she adds. So, your safest bet is a capsule.

#4703. Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 12:05 PM EST

While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took issue with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered new approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”

“I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup said in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”

It took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”

Instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen said this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

“This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

But does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” said Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”

Okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he said. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”

#4701. Kia went from this one quirky EV 40 years ago to an entire electric lineup

The Kia Besta EV hit the roads in 1986 as the brand’s first fully electric vehicle. 40 years later, Kia continues to “lead the pack” with a full lineup of EVs ranging from entry-level cars and SUVs to three-row models, and just about everything in between.

Kia wanted to design a new vehicle for the 1986 Asian Games, which were held in Seoul, South Korea, one that did not emit any toxic fumes in front of runners.

So, it created the Besta EV. The Besta van was initially developed 40 years ago by Kia’s Central Research Institute as the successor to the popular Bongo van, which is still sold in Korea and other markets today.

Unlike the Bongo, it was developed using Kia’s in-house tech rather than sourced from another automaker and rebadged as its own.

Kia swapped the 2.0L four-cylinder diesel engine for a 35 kWh battery and electric motor, which provided a range of more than 26 miles (42 km) on a single charge.

While the Besta EV was never actually sold to the public, it laid the groundwork and offered an early glimpse at Kia’s shift to electrification.

The first mass-produced Korean EV certified for commercial sale was the Kia Pride EV in 1993. In 2011, the Ray EV became Kia’s first series-production electric car.

Kia expanded its electrification ambitions to Europe and the UK in 2014 with the first-generation Soul EV, the beloved boxy, funky crossover that was discontinued after the 2025 model year.

The Korean automaker has come a long way since the Besta EV, with a full lineup of electric vehicles ranging from compact cars to mid-size and three-row SUVs, vans, and just about everything in between.

Kia now offers an electric option for nearly everyone with seven-passenger EVs on sale in the UK and Europe, including the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 Passenger van.

With its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) and a new B-segment electric hatchback set to launch by the end of 2027, Kia has no plans to slow down. On top of this, Kia will expand its PBV lineup with the PV7 next year, a larger sibling to the PV5.

Four decades after the Besta EV arrived, Kia said it continues to “lead the pack today” with one of the most diverse all-electric EV lineups of any brand.

Through October, Kia has sold over 135,000 EVs in the UK, with fully electric vehicles now accounting for over 37% of total sales.

Thanks to its new EV lineup, Kia became “Europe’s fastest-growing top 10 passenger-car brand.” According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Kia registered 377,078 vehicles between January and August 2026, up 9% compared to the same period last year.

Sjoerd Knipping, Chief Operating Officer of Kia Europe, said the growth is thanks to having “one of the broadest and most advanced electrified line-ups in Europe.”

In the US, Kia launched the compact EV3 (check out our review of it) this year, starting at just $29,890. It joins the EV6, EV9, and Niro EV in Kia’s US electric vehicle lineup.

#4699. First albatross egg of the season spotted at Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 2:03 PM EST

Nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

One special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

#4698. 5 Best Hotel Sheets for a Boutique Bedscape (2026)

We want to let you in on a secret: You can replicate the good night’s rest you get at luxury destinations by dressing your bed with the hotel-quality sheets. Aside from accessories like fluffy down feather pillows and mattress toppers, we often attribute cotton percale and sateen to a five-star sleep.

To get down to the nitty-gritty of these sheets, a hotel bed dressed in a percale weave boasts a crisp look and feel, almost as if it were made from your favorite pressed button-down shirt. A sateen weave, however, is polished and resembles the appearance of pearls. What’s more, both of these high-quality sheets have breathable, wrinkle-resistant qualities for a refined aesthetic we know and love in a high-end establishment.

Many of our favorite places to buy bedding—including Italian luxury brands like Frette—even create custom bed linens like these for the best hotels around the world. Scroll below for a staycation-style set of sheets.

For consistency, all of the prices reflect queen sizes. However, many brands offer twin size and king size options too.

The Andersen Hotel, a family-owned boutique retreat in Copenhagen, offers guests sheets, towels, and robes from the editor-favorite brand Boll & Branch. To mimic the experience at home, you can shop the entire collection, including the Signature Hemmed Sheet Set tested and beloved by contributor Rachel Fletcher. The buttery-soft cotton sateen set is made with long-staple cotton fibers, and only gets softer with each wash. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, makes them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” Fletcher shares. After more than five years with these sheets, Fletcher adds that there are no signs of pilling or wear, “just that coveted softness which feels lived-in but not worn out.”

Matouk is a legacy brand known for bespoke touches on high-thread-count sheets. Their hotel collection is found in a number of luxury resorts and historic inns, including Hotel Barrière Fouquet's in New York City and renowned Arizona wellness escape Castle Hot Springs. The Bergamo is their most lightweight percale sheet, combining Giza 87 and 92 Egyptian cotton yarns. “I hate scratchy sheets, and I breathed a sigh of relief when I slipped into these,” says contributor Allie Weiss. “They are lightweight, crisp-looking, and soft to the touch.” We also recommend taking advantage of their personalization feature, which allows you to add a monogram to the edge of the sheet. Just remember that each piece is sold separately, so you’ll have to build your own bedscape.

Another property with Frette bedding, The Palace Hotel in Madrid is an AD-favorite historic hotel. “You’ll definitely want to stop by La Cúpula during your trip for an afternoon drink and some bites from the stylish tapas menu,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “If it’s the right time of day, the room becomes drenched in sunlight through the dome-shaped stained glass ceiling.” As for the bedding, you can mirror the hotel’s lavish interiors with Frette’s bold sheets. The polished sateen set boasts a thick border in six color combinations to wake up a bedroom.

Make a statement without sacrificing a classic hotel look with this tuxedo sheet set. Crafted by Frette for the Ritz-Carlton, this design includes a white-on-white stripe pattern that is perfect for a suite-inspired space. For a unique touch, you can also pair a set of the classic pillowcases with this set for a blend of solid colors and bold lines. Instead of shorter threads that can fray over time, this fabric is made of extra-long staple cotton sateen for an ultra-soft and durable feel.

Priding themselves on a sustainable outlook toward hospitality, the 1 Hotel Group offers a connection with nature and serenity even in the heart of the city. With green-certified buildings and a focus on wellness, it’s no surprise that this hotel’s bedding is equally natural. Kassatex’s 100% cotton sheets are softer than percale but not as shiny as sateen. Contributor Kate McGregor stayed at the 1 Hotel Seattle and was impressed with the breathability. “I’m quite a hot sleeper, but even after a cross-country flight, I slept soundly,” she says. “There was no swishing noise as I moved, either, a pet peeve of mine with really crisp hotel sheets.” Machine washable and available in either a queen or king set, these sheets come with a 60-day trial, so you can really get a feel for them without worrying about a wasted investment.

What Type of Sheets Do Five-Star Hotels Use?

While it varies from property to property, the majority of the hotels on this list use white cotton sheets. Whether percale or sateen, the best hotel sheets all offer a neat, design-agnostic look that suits the center of New York just as well as the rolling hills of Tuscany. Percale will have an added crispness and cooling factor, while sateen will have an added shine and smoothness. Regardless of material finish, look for an all-natural fiber makeup (like 100% cotton) and a versatile white colorway.

Why Do Hotels Like to Use White Bed Sheets?

From an aesthetic perspective, white sheets offer a cloudlike, serene escape for the guest. They also look the cleanest. Stark white sheets cannot hide stains or wear and tear as darker colors can—you can see exactly where each thread has snagged. White bedding is also the most easily sanitized; it even has its own setting on your washing machine. Bleach is necessary to kill germs, especially in a commercial setting, and you don’t want to risk the color fading and yellow stains that can occur on colored sheets.

What Type of Sheets Does The Ritz-Carlton Use?

The Ritz-Carlton uses white cotton sheets from luxury bedding brand Frette. The extra-long staple cotton is more durable than short strands, proven wash after wash. Boasting a subtle monochromatic stripe, The Ritz-Carlton’s sheets play with texture without departing from the clean lines and opulent energy of their suites' overall design scheme.

What Fabrics Are the Best Sheets Made of?

Long or extra-long-staple cotton sheets are considered the “best,” in our experience. These typically have a smooth finish and hold up well over time. That said, so much of it comes down to your own personal preferences. “[Deciding] which one is best for a particular person or climate is relative,” Katie Glusica, professor in the fibers department at the Savannah College of Art and Design, previously shared. “A percale in the 200 to 400 thread-count range will be durable and have a cooler sensation and a lighter weight feel, best for people who run a little warm or where the climate is warmer. Sateen sheets in the 300- to 600-thread-count range are best for someone looking for softness over durability, and better for cooler climates where a heavier feeling sheet is more comfortable.” Then, there are the more seasonal fabrics like airy linen for summer or thick flannel for winter. If you’re still undecided, we often find that Goldilocks-level comfort in cotton sheets with thread counts between 200 and 600 threads per inch.

What Are the Best Bed Sheets for Hot Sleepers and Cold Sleepers?

While percale is recommended for hot or warm sleepers, compared to other cotton sheets, shopping writer Julia Harrison argues the best is bamboo or Tencel lyocell. “AD editors and I prefer these natural fibers because they usually feel cool and gentle against skin, but they also have great temperature regulating qualities since the fabric absorbs excess moisture to help you stay refreshed while you sleep,” she says.

And during the winter months, or for those who run cold year-round, there’s nothing more comforting than sinking into a bed dressed in flannel sheets. “These are great for keeping you cozy and toasty because of a brushed (and sometimes double-brushed) cotton material that feels soft to the touch,” says senior shopping editor Nashia Baker. “It depends on the brand, but some make their sheets with 100% long-staple cotton, like supima cotton, that’s known for its durability without wear over time.”

What Is the Difference Between Percale and Sateen?

Both are made from cotton, but the weave is what differentiates the two. “Percale is a classic one-over, one-under construction that creates a crisp, breathable fabric with a matte finish reminiscent of fine poplin shirting, while sateen’s longer thread float produces a smoother hand and subtle sheen,” Rebecca Weinstein, vice president of design at Highgate, the management company for the Atlas Hotel in Boston, previously told AD. Hot sleepers will feel most comfortable in cooling sheets like percale, while those who prefer a less structured, smooth feel will likely splurge on sateen. “Sateen is more dense, with more threads packed in, so the fabric is warmer,” shared Preeti Gopinath, associate professor of textiles and founding director of the MFA textiles program at Parsons School of Design in New York. “Percale is cooler, and with a thread count of 150 to 200, there is less fabric per square inch, which allows for better airflow.”

#4697. The 22 Best Movies Based on True Stories

IT’S A SUBHEAD that means something and at the same time absolutely nothing. The text appears on screen during trailers and sometimes before the first images of the movie: “based on a true story.” Are there legal criteria for the label? Do producers have guidelines, rules to follow in order to slap the claim onto advertising? Nope. Not that we could find.

Back in 2007, the Los Angeles Times ran something of an informal rule set for the label, which included general principles of straying from fact only if it were to enhance storytelling, but even these guidelines allow for pretty much anything, and the article noted the power of purposeful deceit, like when filmmakers avoided the “realist trap” altogether and nosedived into pure fiction.

What makes a ranking of these films so difficult, then, is that there are so many degrees of “based on a true story.” Are we talking about movies that make this claim, or movies that don’t have to make this claim because it’s so obvious, or movies that both don’t make this claim and yet also somehow find themselves in a half-truth historical territory?

Biopics—films about historical persons—are obviously all based on true stories insofar as their primary character did in fact live and eat and poop, at some moment in time. To include these films, however, would make our list almost endless, since Hollywood loves a good biopic, and because there are so many of them. (Sidenote: Hollywood loves anything that reeks of verisimilitude and has been cranking out true-ish stories at a seemingly increasing rate over the last couple decades).

And so our problem: there are too many damn films.

Our solution: no biopics. Also, we’re skewing a bit more modern with our list. We’re also going to be a little snobby. We’re going with a narrow category of “based on a true story.” That is: movies where the creators went further than simply adapting a book or article. These are movies that employ cinematic techniques that make their work stand apart from the original medium. Sometimes, these works question the veracity of the original story. Other times they find totally different ways of telling the same story, making use of all of film’s particular advantages.

Another question we’re asking: Would it be a good movie if it wasn’t true? Zero Dark Thirty, Selma, The Imitation Game, Spotlight, Nomadland, etc. etc. Great true stories put to screen? Yes. Great movies if they were depicting totally fictional events? Ehhhh.

Obviously, there's a lot to choose from. We did our best.

Here are the best movies based on true events.

Let's start with something pretty uncontroversial. At least, in terms of its praise. Based on the life of T. E. Lawrence, the film is epic in every sense of the word, a treat not just for fans of history but for connoisseurs of cinema. Never again will we probably see that level of practical set pieces and horse riding on screen. Based on history, the film itself has become something of its own historical moment.

Roma is the Speak, Memory of cinema: an artfully crafted autobiography that bucks its own conventions. Here, Mexican filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón choses to disregard his own experiences. Instead, the filmmaker focuses on his former live-in housekeeper, a Mixteco woman who held his family together during marriage turmoil. Call it contemporary neorealism or abstract autofiction or whatever. It's a masterpiece.

The source material for director Adam McKay's finance thriller is Michael Lewis' book of the same name. And the source material for that is, well, the financial crisis. What makes McKay's film so good is tone and form. It veers into meta storytelling without being too heavy-handed. And into humor and comedy without being obnoxiously ironic. It gets the facts right, but it does so in a way that also gets the emotions right.

Chronicling the rise of the so-called Golden Age of Porn, Boogie Nights didn't need to do much tonal alteration to make the story sing. Based on the pornstar John Holmes', er, eccentricities, Paul Thomas Anderson's classic somehow both gets to be one of the best movies of the '90s as well as, in some ways, true to life.

As noted with The Big Short, it's not just the story itself we talk about when we talk about adaptation. It's the form. Dunkirk could have been a straight-laced chronological retelling of the Battle of Dunkirk. Instead, director Christopher Nolan takes a more ambitious approach: manipulating time and chronology in order to capture the feeling of the fight, how such important global events came down to small choices—and tiny, almost banal individual heroics.

We should put some "true crime" on this list. (We actually have a whole separate list for this category, but, ya know.) Adapted from reporter Roberto Saviano's insane investigative work of the same name, Gomorrah avoids all cinematic theatrics for a sobering look at Neapolitan crime. If The Godfather is Shakespeare, Gomorrah is Dickens.

If you want a case study in "based on a true story," watch Netflix's 22 July and Norway's Utøya: July 22. Both depict the 2011 mass shooting at the summer camp on Utøya island, which left over 60 children dead. The American version choses a more removed approaching, telling the larger story of the attacks. The Norwegian version choses a kind of subjective impressionism, depicting only the hours of the shooting and filmed in a one-take style. It's probably the most horrifying thing you will ever watch and, we think, a masterclass in historical adaptation.

Another mass shooting movie? Yep. Gus Van Sant's Elephant isn't explicitly about the Columbine school shooting, although the parallels are difficult to ignore. Like Utøya: July 22, the approach is impressionistic, putting viewers inside the school, drifting its cold, unfeeling camera down hallways and into classrooms. No other film has better captured an event that remains, tragically, all too relevant.

Cinema has more realism tricks than the found-footage style of the above entries. One, surprisingly, is animation. Unlike live action, animation can visualize abstraction without bending into uncanny CGI; because the style is consistent, artists are able to twist images without readers being pulled out of the work. Based on one soldier's experiences during the 1982 Lebanon War, Waltz With Bashir does exactly this. It probes memory, visualizing trauma and torment like only animation can.

We're going to keep saying the word "impressionistic" on this list, so we should probably define it. While some artistic styles seek clear verisimilitude—depicting things as they might have seen from without—impressionistic filmmaking is an attempt at phenomenology, capturing what it must be like from within. "From within" best explains The Diving Bell and the Butterfly, which is based on the story of Jean-Dominique Bauby who, at 43, suffered a seizure which caused "locked-in syndrome," meaning, for the rest of his life, he could only see and hear, but not move. The film does its best to capture this from Bauby's perspective. The result is magic.

We haven't really had a straight adaptation on this list yet. So here it is. All the President's Men is based on the book of the same name by reporters Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward. The result is an equally sobering account of the Watergate political scandal. No style over substance here. Just great dramatization. While there are notable contemporary examples of this approach to "based on a true story," we're going to limit this list to just this one. Sorry, Spotlight.

Right. So we said no biopics. And it's arguable how biopic this biopic biopics. If anything, Nicolas Winding Refn's visualization of one violent inmate's incarceration stands as a great example of successful bombast—totally disregarding a viewer's need of objective clarity and just going full bat-shit impressionism on a story. We appreciate it.

Less stylistic than Bronson, but more than All the President's Men, Steve McQueen's 2013 Oscar winner is maybe the perfect iteration of this form. What is real remains real, and what wasn't real but probably could have been real also feels real. Which is to say: We accept everything we see. And we feel it. For another great historical adaptation from McQueen, check out Hunger.

What begins as a seemingly clear adaptation of persons and events evolves into something far more interesting, challenging, and narratively complex. A Beautiful Mind shines as an adapted story because of its trickery, its commitment to its protagonist—not only to his life but his experience of that life.

As with Waltz With Bashir, studio Ghibli's adaptation (here, a short story about the 1945 firebombing of Kobe) challenges what we expect from "true story" mediums. One might think animation removes readers from the horrors of the events depicted, but it's actually the opposite: somehow, the contrast between the seemingly puerile style of animation and the horror these characters experience makes the film all the move gutting.

Why? you ask. Because! Say what you will about the film's melodrama and tear-bating, James Cameron's Titanic just ... works. It's pure historical fiction; nothing in this movie is real besides the ship and the iceberg. Still, Cameron finds a way to make movie magic out of the event. Remember what we said about diverging from fact in order to serve storytelling? That's exactly what's happening here. These choices work. And they work even better when the audience has some historical footing to stand on.

It may be one of the most straightforward adaptations on this list—in that the film isn't playing too much with form, information, or reality. Still, Spielberg's (best?) film is not simply documentary. The movie finds the director at the height of his storytelling powers, using the story of Oskar Schindler to attempt something much bigger: making sense of modern history's most unfathomable crimes.

Right. So The Wrestler isn't a biopic. Nor is it explicitly based on a true story. Why is it on here? Because Darren Aronofsky's depiction of late-career Randy "The Ram" Robinson (fake) is something like a pastiche of similar real life stories. Aronofsky drew from several in order to craft The Wrestler's central character. Which, in a way, makes the story more real than many realize, even if its mostly false. The parts that are real hit you even harder, like a folding chair to the spine.

A final entry for animation. Mary and Max uses stop motion to tell the story of two real penpals, the Australian filmmaker (Adam Elliot) and a New Yorker living with Asperger syndrome. As with the other animated entries on here, the film makes use of its medium to do what live action can't. In this case, the stop motion form enhances the eccentricities of the characters, while also providing unexpected windows to hit viewers with those #Feels.

If there were any ramifications to the "based on a true story" tagline Hollywood loves so much, then Oliver Stone's JFK would be making attorneys work some long hours. The film is, well, let's just say it's sort of speculative, bordering on conspiratorial. But that's what the story of the JFK assassination is, too. The film doesn't necessarily capture the event so much as the discourse around it, and, in that sense, forges a different kind of accuracy.

Joshua St Clair is an Assistant Editor at Men's Health Magazine.
