#4695. 16 Best Strength Training Exercises to Build Muscle and Strength Fast

There’s no shortage of strength training exercises to pepper into your muscle-building routine. If you’re a regular on FitTok, you might’ve noticed that a new exercise seems to pop up regularly. So, which ones should you pepper into your routine?

“It all comes down to your goal,” says Angela Gargano, a trainer and creator of Strong Feels Good & Pull-up Revolution. The exercises you fill your program with are your most important tools for success.

Keep reading for the best strength training exercises to try, exactly how to add them into a total-body routine, and expert-backed tips for making a plan that works. Ready to get lifting?

Build lasting strength with the WH+ Strong Over 50 Plan, here

Below, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite strength training exercises, spanning all the different muscle groups. Here’s how to create a well-rounded full-body routine you can do regularly.

Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance band | Good for: Total body Instructions: Pick one move from each category—push, pull, hinge, lunge, squat—to create a total body workout. Do it two to three days a week, preferably on nonconsecutive days. For each move, do the allocated amount of sets and reps, resting for 1 to 2 minutes between sets. Select weights that make the last few reps challenging, but doable (and more on selecting weights, below!).

Alternatively, you can split up muscle groups if you have multiple days a week to work out (if you’re working out only two days a week or less, stick with a full-body plan). There are a few ways to do this. If you're planning on strength training twice a week, you can also opt to do one upper-body day (the push/pull exercises) and one lower-body day (the hinge/lunge/squat exercises). Select four or five exercises with a variety of exercise type (don’t fill a lower body day with only squats, no matter how much you love them!) to create your workout.

Or, if you're working out three times a week, you can split your workouts to do one push/pull day, and two hinge/lunge/squat days, or vice versa, depending on what part of your body you want to strengthen most. If you're training more than three times a week, you can split by muscle group.

Here are 16 of the best strength training exercises to fill in your workout.

Why it rocks: Pushups are a classic move for a reason: They work your chest, shoulders, and triceps. Another perk? They engage your core muscles and build functional strength.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 or 4 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Unlike a standard shoulder press, this upper-body exercise challenges all three muscle heads of your deltoids.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Triceps extensions are killer for isolating and strengthening your triceps muscles for improved strength and functionality.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: You’ll strengthen your lats, traps, and delts with this classic upper-body pull move. The bent-over position provides a little extra challenge to your core, too.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps.

Why it rocks: This is an excellent bent-over row variation that targets your lats and rhomboids, requiring less core stability than a traditional bent-over row.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: You’ll strengthen your lats, traps, and delts with this upper-body movement. “This exercise is so beneficial because you are working in a hinged position and teaching your body how to properly brace,” Harvey notes. “This will come in handy the next time you need to bend over and pick something up.”

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Deadlifts build overall strength and power in the posterior chain muscles, including the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps.

Why it rocks: This move strengthens your lower body while also improving stability, and the resistance band is great for added intensity.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: This beginner-friendly move works your glutes, core, and lower back, and may help mitigate back discomfort due to sitting.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 8 to 10 reps.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges work the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes, all while improving coordination and stability.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: Curtsy lunges torch the glutes and outer thighs, while also improving lower body strength and muscle symmetry.

Why it rocks: In addition to working your outer glute muscles and upper legs, this move helps promote stability and balance in your lower body.

Why it rocks: Holding an object like a kettlebell (though you can also use a dumbbell) at chest height calls your core more in on the action—training your body proper core activation that will allow you to push heavier as you get stronger.

Why it rocks: The Bulgarian split squat can shore up functional strength unilaterally, helping to correct any imbalances.

Strength training can help you build and maintain muscle mass, improve your joint and bone health, support better body composition, and even increase your longevity. And, including it in your routine is easy to do, as long as you follow these tips and tricks.

“The biggest thing in putting together your entire workout is making sure that you have a proper warm-up, always, no matter what,” says Gargano. “People tend to throw that out the window but dynamic moves are going to help you wake the body up a little bit before you get into your strength training.”

To execute a proper warm-up, select 3 to 4 dynamic and mobility exercises (these are a few of our favorites!) and do them for 30 seconds apiece, 2 or 3 times through. If you're planning on exercising a specific part of your body that day, make sure your warm-up is tailored to that (e.g., if you're about to do a leg day lift, select a few warm-up moves that promote blood flow to the lower body, like lateral lunges or the World's Greatest Stretch).

“In your programming, there’s a combination of things you should always have,” says Gargano, noting you don’t have to put them all in the same workout/day, but they should certainly all fit in your week: Push movements (like pushups and chest presses), pull movements (like pull-ups and rows), squats, lunges, and hinge movements (think: deadlifts, hip hinges).

Programming your workouts will largely depend on how many times a week you work out (more on that here). The more times a week you can exercise, the more you can split your workouts by muscle group. For example, if you're working out three days per week, you might be interested in doing one upper-body day, one leg day focused on glutes and hamstrings, and another focused on quads and calves. If you're only working out twice per week, you'll want to make sure you're programming for the whole body: at least one upper-body lift and one lower-body lift.

“I know people are going to be like, ‘Well, what about my core?’ but your core is used in all those movements,” Gargano assures.

“You want to be sure that you're working all the body parts so that you're not uneven,” says Gargano. It's an issue trainers see a lot—people focus so hard on defining one part of their body that they neglect the rest. For example, if you're aiming to build up your glutes, don't only do hip thrusts on lower body day. Incorporate some lunges and squats in there, too, to strengthen your quad muscles so they can work in tandem with your strong glutes.

As long as you hit all five of the main movement patterns we named earlier (push, pull, squat, lunge, hip hinge) throughout the week, you should be in good shape.

A few weeks into your workout program, your body will get used to what you’re doing—so you'll need to level up the challenge, “so that your body can continue to develop and work the muscles in different ways,” says Gargano. That means increasing your weights, reps, or sets to progressively overload the muscles—doing so will help them get continuously stronger, and ensure your performance never plateaus.

To know when to up the weights, use the two-for-two rule: Once you can do two extra good-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load. From there, try to increase 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. But remember, this is just a recommendation—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

The best exercise plan is the one you're going to stick to. And the one you're going to stick to is the one that best fits into your schedule.

“You need to figure out what is working well for you and your body,” says Gargano. “Everybody's different, so try out two days a week first, and then if you feel good, maybe add that third day.”

Once you have your schedule set, don't feel like it's an end-all, be-all. The more you can hit your workouts, the better—but there's no reason to knock yourself down if things get busy and you miss one or two. You can always abbreviate your workout by cutting a few exercises or sets, or get moving by going for a brief walk. The key is to stay moving as much as you can. It won't always be perfect, and that's okay.

Marcel Dinkins, CPT, is a New York-based certified personal trainer and Peloton Tread instructor. Angela Gargano, CPT, is a certified trainer and creator of Strong Feels Good & Pull-up Revolution.

#4693. South Korea will use emergency alert system to warn about exam cheaters

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:10 PM EST

On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with new tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

The sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han says he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place new anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin quickly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be new concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

#4691. Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health. When I’m not writing, editing, and researching fitness, I’m teaching it to my personal training and group fitness clients. In my new column, Between Sets, I’m pulling back the curtain on the same advice, tips, and ‘aha!’ moments I share with my clients while they’re catching their breath. Stick around for the strategic, science-backed nuggets that’ll help you move better, train smarter, and actually enjoy the process.

Scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy. And where there’s real joy in getting stronger, there’s also real pressure to keep adding weight.

As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years. For valid reason: challenging your muscles over time is one of the most reliable ways to build lasting strength, support bone health, improve body composition, and stay functional as we age.

The “lift heavy” ethos isn’t new. Strength training is as old as Ancient Greece, where the first gyms were developed. It progressed through decades of physical culture into Muscle Beach, USA, the birthplace of American lifting that started as a beachside gymnastics park in Venice Beach, California, in the 1940s. It was there, too, where the first American women bodybuilders, like legendary Abbey Stockton, emerged—at a time when many scientists still believed lifting was bad for the body.

Research eventually caught up to what lifters were already experiencing: resistance training works. More women, especially in recent years, started showing up for it, too. In 2004, 17 percent of women reported regularly participating in weight lifting. By 2020, that number has bumped to nearly 30 percent. Then came the influencer era, amplifying a message that’s equal parts motivating and misleading: lifting weights is good for you—but it has to be heavy to count.

There’s a kernel of truth in there. Progressive overload (the process of gradually increasing the stress you put on your body in a workout) builds muscle and strength, and increasing load is an efficient way to do so.

And that matters—especially when heavier, heavier, heavier simply isn’t in the cards.

Because for many, it’s not. It requires access to specific equipment, time to train consistently without rushing through sets, and quality coaching and information to nail form and stay injury-free. It also has to be safe and appropriate for your body on any given day—whether you’re navigating chronic illness, postpartum or perimenopause realities, and injury history, or limiting pain. And even when everything lines up on paper, there’s a very real mental hurdle: walking into a gym and loading up a bar can be intimidating as hell.

Still, if you’re here to build strength, change your body composition, protect your bone health, or invest in your movement longevity, lifting heavier will certainly help—but it’s not the only path to lifelong strength. Somewhere along the way, “heavy” became synonymous with “effective”, and “light” or "moderate" became codes for “waste of time.”

The exercise research world is finding that’s not the case. “You don't need to do anything heavy for the health benefits of resistance exercise to take place,” says Stuart Phillips, PhD, kinesiology professor and hypertrophy researcher at McMaster University.

Adequate research has suggested that hypertrophy (the fancy scientific term for muscle growth) is not determined by a magic rep goal or the weight on the bar, says Susie Reiner, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, assistant professor of exercise science at Seton Hall University, and CEO of TheoryEx, a sport science research and consulting firm. “Instead, hypertrophy appears to be driven by whether a training set provides a sufficiently strong internal stimulus to the muscle, which is reasonably defined as effort and proximity to muscular failure.”

Trainers have traditionally been taught that specific rep ranges map neatly to specific goals: 1 to 3 for power, 3 to 8 for strength, 8 to 12 for muscle, and 12-plus for muscular endurance. But newer findings show you can build muscle across a much wider rep range—roughly as low as 5 and as high as 25, Phillips says. “There is, then, by definition, no sweet spot for muscle building, because the whole repetition range then becomes the sweet spot.”

Across several studies and meta-analyses, similar muscle growth has been seen between people who train with lighter loads (about 30 to 40 percent of their one-rep maximum), and those who train with heavier loads (about 70 to 85 percent of their one-rep maximum)—as long as sets are taken close enough to failure.

Muscle growth is dependent on recruiting and fatiguing a large portion of muscle fibers, Reiner says. Your muscles need a reason to adapt. With heavier weights for fewer reps, you recruit a lot of fibers immediately. With lighter weights for higher reps, you recruit them more gradually.

One thing to note here: while a large percentage of these studies have only been done in men, Phillips notes that “the work that has been done in women shows us that actually men and women respond very, very similarly to weight lifting in terms of muscle mass gain. Women have less baseline muscle, but relatively speaking, they gain the same amount as men—that's been robustly shown.” Phillips and his colleagues are currently running several studies (including one study specific to perimenopausal women!) that will further clarify what this looks like in women.

Researchers feel confident that as long as sets are taken sufficiently to failure (more on what that means coming up), different loading strategies can produce similar hypertrophy, Reiner says.

Here’s what that looks like IRL: Let’s say you have biceps curls on your workout plan each week. One week, you pick up the 10-pound dumbbells, and do 3 sets of 12 reps. In the sets, when you approach the end of that rep range, it feels tough—you can maybe grind out 2 more reps max. The next week, you reach for the 15s. You can only hit 6 reps before you feel like your form is faltering, but the effort feels similar—you’ve still got about two reps left before your form breaks down.

The heavier weight might feel more empowering, but both workouts deliver a similar muscle-building stimulus—assuming you’re training regularly enough, eating enough protein and calories, and adequately recovering, of course.

Sure, research confirms you don’t have to lift crazy heavy—but that doesn’t mean that coming close to failure feels easy. Failing a rep can be scary (and honestly, discouraging). Here’s the good news: you don’t need true, all-out failure. You just need to train to proximity to failure.

One practical way to gauge that is with the rate of perceived exertion scale. “Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) is a global effort scale, typically ranging from one to 10,” Reiner says. An RPE of 10 represents maximal effort—no chance you could do one more rep. A RPE of nine suggests you could do one more, an RPE of eight means you could probably do two more reps, and so on and so forth.

Muscle growth still occurs between RPE of 7 to 9, Phillips says. “You don’t need it to be a 10 out of 10 where you’re red-lining and can’t get the bar off your chest.” In other words: you can train hard without routinely hitting the point where things get sketchy.

That matters, because the closer you get to all-out failure, the more your injury risk can creep up—especially if you start twisting, bouncing, and compensating to force a rep you simply don’t have.

The failure you want to flirt with is technical failure, or technical fatigue. “Technical failure means you cannot complete another repetition with good form,” Phillips says—that’s where injury risk rises. Muscular failure (otherwise known as momentary failure) occurs when a muscle is unable to generate enough force to complete another rep, regardless of maximal effort. Picture trying to do one more biceps curl and you quite literally cannot lift your arm and the weight up again—that’s muscular failure..

Aim for technical failure. Pushing yourself too far in an effort to achieve muscular failure could cause your body to overcompensate and push you into a compromising position. The good news, too, is technical failure tends to be very close to muscular failure for most people, Phillips says.

A useful rule of thumb: stop when you have one to two perfect-form reps left in the tank.

Yes, you still need to reach for that RPE of 7 to 9—but there’s more ways to do that than just reaching for the next highest weight. Here are some other elements you can play with to up the challenge:

Frequency. Reaching for heavier weights, you can simply aim to reach for any type of weight more often. That might look like increasing your strength training days from two to three days a week.

Volume. Think of your training volume as the amount of weight total you lift during a given session. Sure, lifting heavier loads is one way to increase your total, but it can also be accomplished by increasing the amount of sets or reps you do.

Rest time. Decreasing the amount of rest you allow yourself gives your muscles less time to recover, wearing them out quicker with lighter loads.

Time under tension. The amount of time your muscles work for matters. Increasing your time under tension, or the amount of time your muscles are working in a lift (for example, lowering a curl for a slow four-count).

That all being said, heavier loads might still take the cake in terms of efficiency. You’ll find yourself increasing your frequency and volume to monotonous levels if you never increase your load.

Back to biceps curls: Say you get comfortable at six reps at 15 lbs. After a few weeks, it no longer starts to feel challenging for you, so you increase it eight. And then 10. And then 12. If you never reach for the intimidating 20 lb dumbbells, you’ll eventually find yourself having to do sets of 30 reps just to feel something. And that can become time consuming. You don’t need extremes all the time—but you do need your training to stay challenging.

“For individuals who are uncomfortable training to very high levels of effort, consistent training at moderate-to-high RPEs combined with sufficient volume and progression can still produce meaningful muscle growth,” Reiner says. “From a long-term perspective, hypertrophy depends less on any single maximal set and more on repeated exposure to challenging, well-managed training over weeks and months.”

Convinced to start pushing closer to failure? Here are a few ways to progress safely.

The two-for-two method is a classic progression strategy used by professional trainers. Once you can do two extra proper-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load.

Let's use the biceps curl example just one more time. You’ve been training with the 15s for sets of 8, and now you can hit 10 with clean form for two workouts in a row. That’s your cue to grab 17.5s the next go.

How much should you increase, exactly? The National Strength and Conditioning Association’s guideline is 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. Reminder that this is just a general guide—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Trying heavier weights is way less intimidating when you have a safety net.

If you’re nervous, ask for a spot. Maybe you already have a gym buddy you workout with regularly that can help pull the barbell up if you get stuck on a bench press. If you don’t, ask one of your gym’s trainers or employees. Most people will politely oblige, and will even appreciate your effort in challenging yourself.

Have a conversation with your spotter before you get into the lift. Tell them how many reps you’re aiming for, and a cue you’ll give them when you want them to jump in and help (my go-to is a simple “now”—since that’s about all you can get out when you’re out of breath).

Some days just don’t feel as strong as others. Maybe you didn’t sleep super well last night, stressed about work, or are at a tough point in your cycle. That’s life. When that happens, you need to respect the cues your body gives you.

If your warmup sets feel unusually heavy, take the hint: this just might not be the day to pick up that heavy weight. It doesn’t mean you’ve regressing, it’s just a bump in the road. Strength, and muscle building, is not a linear process.

Build muscle with the WH+ Build & Burn series

Ultimately, building and maintaining muscle mass is one of the strongest investments you can make in long-term health—especially as you age.

And lifting heavy is one effective way to provide muscle-building stimulus to the body—but it isn’t accessible, comfortable, or safe for everyone all the time. The goal is progressive challenge, and lighter loads can deliver that when you train with intention and effort.

“You do not need to lift heavy to build muscle, but you do need to train with intention,” Reiner says. “The best approach is the one that someone can perform consistently, safely, and with enough effort to challenge the muscle over time.”

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

#4690. This Historic Home Is Built Around a Spectacular Light Well That Looks Like a Connect Four Game

Long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets. Washerwomen and their families lived in narrow, two-story houses, and the women would go to the wells every day to hand-wash clothes. It is in this unique part of the city that you’ll find one of architect Raúl Sánchez’s latest projects.

The lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building. From here, you can see the living area, a corner of the kitchen island, the bottom of the blue light well, and the white-painted beams. Santina chairs from the 1970s are by Carlo Sant.

“It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes. We were asked to restore it for a couple and their child,” explains Sánchez. The house faces two streets: Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers. Since there’s a five-foot difference in the elevation of the two streets, Sánchez decided to add a landing at the higher entrance off Granollers, where one flight of stairs descends to a lower level, which opens onto Calle Aiguafreda, and the other ascends to the upper level of the small house, where the bedrooms and a bathroom are located.

In the living room, the floor is made of terra-cotta tiles that echo the traditional clay paving in the home’s garden. A rectangular skylight is offset by 45 degrees from the rest of the room and lacquered in a deep blue, which is complemented by a red reading corner with a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer (Knoll), and a yellow folding screen. Between two Amanta armchairs by Mario Bellini (Hay) there’s an Altar side table by Ewe Studio (Tacchini). In front of them is a C cork stool designed by Jasper Morrison (Vitra). Atollo lamp by Vico Magistretti (Oluce).

Sánchez added a new architectural element: a light well that extends from a skylight on the roof through the full height of the building, illuminating even the ground-floor spaces, some of which are partially below street level. Pierced by a series of circular openings, like a Connect 4 game, and coated in a glossy blue lacquer, the light shaft evokes an ancient well while also serving as a contemporary, poetic, and functional architectural element.

Halfway up the ground floor, the house has a second entrance from the street. Sánchez added a landing there with two flights of steps: one leading down to the living area, the other leading up to the bedrooms and the bathroom.

A light well topped with a skylight runs the full height of the building, illuminating the spaces all the way down to the ground floor. The 45-degree rotation relative to the rest of the structure defines the home’s circulation and breaks up any feeling of predictable regularity. Perforated with circular openings and coated in blue lacquer, it gives the home a spectacular architectural feature.

It also stands out as an organizing feature of the home, thanks to its 45-degree rotation relative to the floor plan. “This rotated geometry allows for the dynamic opening and closing of different perspectives and circulation paths, thereby avoiding a predictable corridor-like effect,” says Sánchez. “The circular openings also allow for views between rooms and across different levels.” Cut into all four sides of the light well, the circles allow natural light to enter from the skylight on the roof. As the sunlight moves across the walls of the light well throughout the day, the spectacular blue lacquer comes to life.

A large, custom-designed installation by Raúl Sánchez Architects runs from the kitchen to the living room, organizing and defining the spaces. Most of it matches the color of the walls, but it transitions from pale-yellow cabinets in the kitchen to lacquered wood in the living room. Ceramic pieces by Catalina Montaña (@hellobigmontana).

A stone countertop with subtle yellow veining plays off the chick-yellow fronts of the kitchen cabinets. The 9091 kettle is by Richard Sapper (Alessi). Skan pendant light (Vibia).

At the foot of the staircase leading to Calle Granollers, the mirrored door to the bathroom offers a unique perspective on the living area and the skylight.

The first floor, which is a compact 431 square feet, is designed as an open space with living and dining areas, a small office, and a kitchen. At its center is the deep-blue light well, a graphic element that punctuates the mostly neutral color scheme. A folding screen made of wood and rice paper is a special feature for one of the owners, who once lived in Japan; it can either connect or separate the office from the living area. A small powder room is positioned at a 45-degree angle so the door can’t be seen from the main living area. Near the Aiguafreda entrance, a kitchen island, also placed on a diagonal, is clad in mirrors, helping to create a sense of lightness and maintaining the open feeling and flow of the space.

A view of the living area from the small office. White and terra-cotta dominate, accented by splashes of color. In the foreground is a Kyoto table by Gianfranco Frattini (Poltrona Frau).

The house is rooted in the history of both its neighborhood and the specific alley where it is located, and the chosen materials engage in a dialogue with the past. On the first floor, terra-cotta tiles echo the traditional clay paving found in the home’s outdoor space. Colorful glazed tiles adorn the sinks and bathroom walls, with reddish-tone lacquers and paints recalling the clay soil long found in nearby orchards. The glossy blue color and circular perforations of the skylight elicit water droplets from a washing well.

The light filtering through the circular openings of the blue light well casts a glow on the vanity, which is partially clad in red ceramic tiles that cover the countertop and extend up to the ceiling.

The Dioscuri wall sconces (Artemide) blend right in with the play of colors and both the round and rectangular shapes in the hallway leading to the bathroom.

“The mirror-like surfaces of the doors and the kitchen island, with their slight distortions, evoke the reflections on the surface of the water,” says Sánchez. “Above all, the renovation has made it possible to preserve all the elements that give the home its character and history while also integrating contemporary, energy-efficient systems.”

The light well, painted entirely in blue, is at once architectural, functional, and playful.

The home’s green installations include an aerothermal system for air-conditioning, heating, and hot water; a new floor slab on the first floor to limit indoor humidity; enhanced thermal insulation in the roof; and improvements to the thermal and acoustic performance of the façades and shared walls. In addition, the skylight opens to take advantage of a thermal stack effect, expelling hot air in the summer while capturing heat in the winter–transforming the project’s central design element into a system that is both functional and contributes to the home’s environmental sustainability. The interior renovation is only the first phase of the project: Sánchez is currently redesigning the narrow garden, a plot that’s 13 feet wide by 98 feet long.

This home tour was first published by Architectural Digest Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

In the child‘s room, primary colors and a 1980s vibe dominate. The Veronica chair is by Afra and Tobia Scarpa (Casas). The AJ lamp is by Arne Jacobsen (Louis Poulsen).

A view into the light well, which provides illumination and ventilation.

A view of the hallway and staircase from the primary bedroom, whose entryway is painted red, setting the stage for the entrance into the room. Extra-large, veined-wood cabinet handles adorn the full-height cabinet fronts. In the foreground, a Reno chair by Federico Correa and Alfonso Milá from 1961. The Dioscuri wall sconce is by Artemide.

The primary bedroom, located under the roof, is bathed in light. The custom built-in storage units (Raúl Sánchez Architects) feature a stepped design, and the spectacular wood handles, with their prominent grain, add a circular geometric pattern to the space.

The house’s arbor gives it a rural charm, especially surprising given its location in the heart of Barcelona.

#4689. Fiona the hippo under 24-hour care after swallowing hat

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:54 PM EST

UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

“Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”

The zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”

On Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”

#4687. The Secrets to Whole-Life Training

A well-rounded fitness routine that will enhance all of your activities and adventures starts with your feet.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s more to getting fit than chasing a PR or sweating through another bootcamp class. The real payoff? Being ready for the next workout, the weekend adventure, the everyday hustle, and all the years ahead.

The key is making different types of exercise work together, rather than relying on any one activity. This multifaceted and well-rounded approach to training means you’re working more than the muscles, because you’re focused on the movements.

When you approach training this way, you’re literally starting from the ground up. “Every single step you take, your foot is the first thing that hits the ground,” says Jen Perez, DC, a chiropractic physician who combines clinical practice and education to help people improve foot health and lower-body function. “It’s the first thing that interfaces with the world around you, what has to be strong and springy when you want to run or jump or dance or ski.”

A whole-life, well-rounded training plan comes down to five essentials, according to Courtney Conley, DC, a best-selling author and chiropractic physician with more than two decades of clinical experience:

Cardio and strength may already be part of your routine, but the others can be easier to overlook; especially because they deliver numerous movement benefits that you may not equate them with. For example, Conley emphasizes that power training isn’t just for athletes; it also has practical life applications. “Getting up and out of your chair, having good reaction time, and making sure you don’t fall if you step off a curb and trip are all part of that category,” she says.

Mobility means moving freely through a full range of motion, while balance helps you adjust to changing surfaces and react when your footing shifts—it isn’t just holding a tree pose. “There are thousands of nerve endings in each foot that help communicate to our brain where we are in space,” Perez explains. That feedback, combined with the feet’s ability to grip the ground, helps keep you steady.

Recovery is what allows your body to benefit from hard training, yet Conley says it’s often ignored: “I think one of the biggest mistakes is that people don’t recover.” Sleep, adequate nutrition, and lighter days that deliberately scale back workout volume or intensity give your body time to adapt and help you come back ready for your next workout.

The work you do in the gym should go beyond just trying to look good and prepare you for the demands of everyday movement. For strength and power work, Conley recommends deadlifts and kettlebell swings to train the hip-hinge pattern, along with farmer’s carries to build strength in the core and lower body. “I love all that functional movement,” she says. “A sled push is also great, because as your heel comes off the ground, you’re hitting all the intrinsic muscles of your foot.”

Certain machine exercises may not seem so functional but can address specific weaknesses. For instance, Conley says she often uses seated calf raises to strengthen the tissues around the Achilles and leg extensions to isolate the quadriceps. She also recommends plyometrics—quick, explosive jumping and hopping drills—to develop power. “Try double-leg and single-leg hops, forward and backward, side to side, and zigzag moves,” she says, recommending five or six sets of 10 reps per exercise for plyometric movements.

Ankle and big-toe mobility are number one on Conley’s priority list for things you should focus on outside of your regular workouts. “When you can’t propel through the ankle, you’re going to get there by extending the knee so you can push yourself forward,” she says. “People come in with knee or back pain when oftentimes it’s an ankle problem.” She suggests making mobility a regular part of the week rather than waiting until something feels stiff or restricted. Even a short dedicated session can help you maintain the range of motion your training requires.

Perez says your feet also adapt to the surface beneath you and absorb force. “If you think of your foot like a trampoline, every single step we take, whether walking or running, the foot needs to be able to lower, which is that mobility piece, then it needs to be able to spring back up.”

Perez recommends two simple drills to improve foot mobility and strength: the Foot Handshake, where you weave the fingers of one hand between the toes of the opposite foot and gently circle the foot at the ankle; and Lift, Spread, and Reach, where you lift all five toes, spread them apart, then reach them forward as you lower them.

Another way you can activate your feet during training is to choose your shoes wisely. When it comes to footwear, Perez has one non-negotiable regardless of the activity: a wide toe box that lets your toes spread naturally. “If your toes are more narrow than the ball of your foot, that tells me we’ve got some work to do,” she says. In practice, that can mean adding foot mobility and strength drills to your routine and choosing shoes that let your toes spread naturally.

Perez favors Altra Fit, both for her own footwear and when recommending shoes to others, because it gives the forefoot more room than a traditionally tapered toe box. Conley’s experience shows how the amount of cushioning that feels right can change over time as your foot gets stronger and needs more targeted footwear. She started out in the Altra FWD VIA 2, a cushioned shoe with the original (read: roomiest) FootShape™ and a 4 mm drop that felt familiar coming from conventional running shoes. “I was getting some toe splay and my foot was getting stronger,” she recalls. “Now I put them on, and it’s too much shoe for me because I don’t need as much cushioning.”

That’s where having options comes in. Altra’s Torin 9 offers a more moderate level of cushioning, standard footshape (secure midfoot), and a zero-drop platform that is good for running and still takes advantage of the Altra Fit that helps your feet get stronger as you log miles. For a lower-profile option, the Altra Escalante 5 has low cushioning, a 24 mm stack height, zero drop, and the original, roomiest FootShape fit.

“You’ll want to use the least amount of shoe assistance necessary for the activity,” Perez recommends. A lower-profile, more flexible shoe, like the Escalante 5, offers more ground feel for strength training, while extra cushioning or rocker geometry, found in the Torin 9 and FWD VIA 2, may be useful on longer runs. Conley agrees that a plush running shoe isn’t necessarily the best tool for lifting. “You can’t feel the ground,” she says of maximalist shoes. “You’re standing on something that decreases your sensory acuity.”

If multidimensional fitness is new to you, Conley recommends starting with manageable strength work (two or three days a week), walking, and one or two mobility or foot exercises, and build gradually as your strength and capacity improve. “Do things that challenge you, but not to the point where you start to feel overwhelmed,” she says.

If you already work out or run regularly, consider what’s missing from your routine while prioritizing your main goal. Conley suggests making room for mobility, balance, and power work, and fitting short foot-strength and mobility exercises into existing workouts. Do it while you’re fresh, adjusting your workload when running volume increases or recovery suffers.

The goal isn’t to do everything all the time or become an expert at every type of training. It’s to build a body that can keep doing the things you love. Run the trails. Lift the heavy stuff. Hike the mountain. Get down on the floor with your kids and grandkids—and have the strength and mobility to get back up again.

#4686. This Designer Finds Unexpected Beauty in Marble’s Leftovers

Wandering through the ruins of Pompeii, the ancient Roman city frozen in time by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, one is struck by that civilization’s devotion to precious materials. Surviving mosaics depict the opulence that once filled the city’s lavish homes. These fragments of classical life, and the richness with which they were rendered, captured the imagination of Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak, inspiring his upcoming Tesserae series for the New York design gallery Ateliers Courbet.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

Kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying new stones,” Kolodziejczak says.

Kolodziejczak with two vessels from his Tesserae series

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz

The designer polishes the base to a console from his Tesserae series.

The remnants accumulated in his studio until, on a visit to Pompeii, he had “the idea to bring them together” in one exhibition. His vessel shapes, inspired by antique Roman pottery, are hand-carved in marble, along with materials like rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz. The series will also include a monumental crystal pendant light, sconces in bronze with citrine quartz shades, a mirror, and massive stone tables. But despite the expansive scale, Kolodziejczak’s sensibility remains rooted in the concept of adornment. “I treat furniture like jewelry,” says the designer, whose Studio Daniel K is based in Milan and Paris. “These pieces aren’t meant to take up the entire room—just to be that accent of something extraordinary.”
