#4645. Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Updated Nov 19, 2026 9:53 AM EST

After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

“The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he says. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”

Astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”

Even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

“Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” says Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”

“Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

As part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

All good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are currently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical issues, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

“Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any new region.”

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an important lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

“Do not be afraid to dream big. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he says. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”

UPDATE November 19 10:00 a.m. EST: An earlier version of this story said light moves at 186,282 feet per second. It is 186,282 miles per second. We have updated unit of measurement and apologize for the error.

#4644. Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

Environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a new, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

“It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, said in a statement.

Wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

The idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

#4643. Aptera (SEV) completes its first customer solar EV — for its top crowdfunder

Aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.

It’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022. And it comes a week after Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash against the roughly $25 million it says it needs to start series production.

Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.

Accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most. So the first customer car went to the biggest check.

Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.

In the release, Hartono said Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the company is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.

The timing is interesting. Just seven weeks ago, Aptera cut its estimated cost to start production to about $25 million, down from $40 to $45 million, and said the first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries in early 2027 “subject to financing.”

Its Q3 report last week didn’t change that picture much. Aptera ended September with $9.2 million in cash, and $4.1 million of that is refundable reservation fees. It lost $14 million in the quarter, and its own filing says substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern “has not been alleviated.”

On November 10, it priced a $6 million registered direct offering at $1.75 per share. SEV closed at $1.67 on Tuesday, with a 52-week high of $7.

The solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.

The release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.

Credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this company since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.

A positive achievement, but the question remains: Is this essentially a hand-built prototype and a token delivery to one very rich customer, or is it the first of many more vehicles that will roll off an assembly line for regular people over the next couple months?

But I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it says it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the company. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.

The real test is still the first 40 cars, and whether they reach regular reservation holders in the US. Aptera says it needs about $25 million to get there. It has $9.2 million, $4.1 million of which customers can ask back for, and it’s raising money at under $2 a share, which means a lot of dilution for every dollar.

We want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?

#4642. Preparing Kids for Their AI Future

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

As you’ve most certainly seen on the news, artificial intelligence (AI) is here, and it’s in the process of changing our society. Depending on your point of view, AI seems to be either a blessing or a curse. Maybe both. While AI may help doctors cure diseases that have plagued us for centuries, it may also be an existential threat to our survival on the planet. The bottom line is, AI is here, and whether it’s the ultimate triumph of technology or the worst creation ever invented is yet to be seen.

While all of the differing reports on AI reverberate through the news cycle, it’s important for parents to know how AI can affect their children. For example, AI has aided in suicides by telling teens effective ways to harm themselves. Obviously, this is an extreme and major mistake. Hopefully, steps are being taken to stop that type of information from being dispensed in the future.

While these types of extreme examples get headlines and are acutely dangerous, there are other dangers that AI brings to children and their education that are not as widely publicized. For example, students can now use AI to do their homework or write their term papers. In the space of a few minutes, students can feed their assignment into AI and voila, out pops a well-written, factually sourced paper. If the student does a little tweaking, it may not be recognizable as AI, and the teacher may accept it as the student’s own work.

While cheating in school is not new, it’s never been this easy to game the system. While this can certainly be appealing to many students, the drawbacks of using AI to cheat carry real risks for their future. Beyond the information they are not learning within the paper they were supposed to write, they are also shirking responsibility. This can harm students by giving them a false sense of security in the present but damaging their ability to deliver what’s necessary in the future.

In any career, meeting deadlines is important. One of the ways in which we all learn to complete tasks within specific time frames is through school projects. If students don’t learn this, it can hold them back in whatever career they pursue. This is just one example of how AI’s seeming help can have long-lasting consequences.

AI is also going to make many jobs unnecessary. A student who doesn’t develop critical thinking skills, as well as specific areas of expertise, becomes an adult who is ripe for being replaced by AI. It seems that people who are able to think creatively, understand how to accomplish tasks efficiently, and learn to follow through on commitments are more likely to maintain careers.

That’s why, as parents, it’s important that we talk with our children about the value of thinking for themselves. If they surrender all of their choices and individuality to AI, they’re likely to become little more than worker drones in perhaps the very near future. The more skilled and resourceful they are, along with building a work ethic that gives them self-esteem and self-confidence, the better prepared they are for the future.

The question becomes, what can we do to help? By sharing with our children the importance of learning and taking responsibility for their own futures, they can be better prepared to deal with whatever changes happen. By building up their self-image and confidence, they can see more possibilities for themselves and be more ready to face the challenges that arise in their lives.

It does not seem to be in the best interest of today’s youth to surrender to the ease of AI. By doing so, they may not be learning vital life lessons, which can undermine their futures. Our children need to know they still have a place in the world and can prepare themselves to thrive no matter what changes may occur.

#4640. The Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach is an electric van built for camping, but it’s not cheap

Volkswagen introduced the ID. Buzz Beach, a fun spin on its electric van that’s built for camping and overnight stays. However, it won’t be cheap, starting at over $70,000.

Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.

The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.

Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.

The new ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen said after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.

Volkswagen said it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.

The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.

In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.

For camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

The ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.

To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.

Volkswagen will open orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK later this month, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it will start at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.

Nice product at the wrong price. If VW can't lower the price because of the cost, then it has a lot more work to do to compete in this market.

What about those in the US? VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with a new Tourer model that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.

However, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be delaying the ID. Buzz’s return until the 2028 model year.

The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.

A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

#4639. Bear cub takes award-winning leap of faith

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 1:05 PM EST

In bear life, as in human life, sometimes you just have to take a leap of faith. A brown bear (Ursus arctos) cub hanging around Anan Creek in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska learned that this summer. Its mom, Gemini, was crossing the creek, and one cub jumped right in. But this cub? Not so sure. It stood waiting at the water’s edge, before jumping in.

For this forceful leap into the water, the park rangers have awarded Gemini’s little cub with the 2026 Yeet of Faith Award. For those keeping score at home, Gemini won this year’s helicopter mom award.

“Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots for wildlife is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears like Gemini and her cubs. Similar to their chubby counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to gorge on salmon ahead of the long winter, and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear around Anan Creek has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behaviors

#4638. Tasting Our Memories

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I’m standing in front of the fish counter at Market Basket, the grocery store chain that serves much of eastern Massachusetts. I scan the cooler for oysters. Shucked oysters, to be specific. It’s the day before Thanksgiving. I’m trying to recreate the menu of my youth. Those offerings included scalloped oysters, a recipe that my mother made every Thanksgiving and Christmas. Mom passed away in 2023. She never wrote down the recipe. She always followed the "handful of this" and a "pinch of that" school of cooking. She was masterful. I, on the other hand, celebrate the occasional culinary win, but more often than not, my successes are hit or miss—especially when it comes to the infrequent concocting of scalloped oysters.

Why do we try so hard, at this time of the year, to recreate the recipes from our past?

We are attempting to do more than recreate those dishes; we are trying to conjure the ghosts of those friends and family members who are no longer with us.

Roast the perfect turkey. Prepare the perfect pumpkin pie. Arrange an artistic nut tray. Make the perfect mashed potatoes with just enough lumps to know they’re homemade, but not so many that we ask, “Who cooked the potatoes?”

Some families carefully divvy the work among invited dinner guests. Auntie will handle the fresh cranberry relish, while Cousin brings the almond green bean casserole. Somehow, two people end up making the candied sweet potatoes, but one looks a little gray while the other is adorned with perfectly toasted mini-marshmallows. We will struggle to consume both. We don’t want to hurt anyone’s feelings.

Are we attempting to make Instagram-worthy dishes for the social media kudos? Or are we endeavoring to improve upon the butter-laden, sugary dishes of our youth? Remember that Uncle Robbie needs to watch his caloric intake after suffering a minor heart attack last spring. And Cousin Joanne is supposed to be watching her sugar since she started taking insulin to control her diabetes.

“It’s just one day,” we counter. “How bad could it be?”

But there are ethical considerations, too. Shannon’s new friend is vegan. Out of respect, we throw together a dairy-free lasagna. Is that really enough?

In-laws bring new traditions. My husband’s grandmother’s family favorite of orange ice befuddles our daughter-in-law’s family, but they agree to serve it every year. “We eat this first?” one asks. “But won’t the turkey get cold?” A question I’ve asked myself for almost fifty years. “Maybe this would be better served for the 4th of July!” someone says. And we all nod. And we never actually follow through.

New Orleanian author Amy Cyrex Sins mourned the absence of a recipe for Doberge cake after losing her treasured recipe file and her home after Hurricane Katrina ravaged Louisiana in August of 2005. While she suffered the obvious loss of possessions, it was the inability to recreate a favored family treat that continued to jab at her with the sharp barbs of loss, both physical and emotional. I remember sharing her essay with an honors college class many years ago. One student took it upon herself to make the dish. We New Englanders had no context to judge her success, but I know that I enjoyed a slice of cake that day. And I’ll never forget how she cut the cake by carving out a center circle and then cutting slices from the outside rim. A new tradition? Probably not. A new taste memory? Definitely.

But tasting our past and our memories encompasses so much more than carefully measuring and mixing ingredients.

When we attempt to recreate recipes from our childhoods and our pasts, we honor those cooks and chefs of our ancestors.

Vera, my maternal grandmother, was a terrible cook. I remember her making hamburgers and boiled potatoes. The patties were overcooked, the potatoes fork-mashed with butter and pepper. That was a staple meal served almost every night of the week! Grammy was a single mother, having been widowed at the age of nineteen. At the time, she was pregnant and had a two-year-old. Survival was critical. Tastes were secondary. And this was during the Great Depression.

One forgives a lack of herbs and spices when cheap ground beef and farm-raised spuds were often rationed between the extended family members of Canadian immigrants.

Psychotherapist and Relationship Expert Mary Pender Greene writes, “Remember that there are NO perfect holidays” (2009, p. 26). She suggests that the malaise of the holidays stems from “unrealistic expectations, which is often inspired by holiday marketing” (Greene, 2009, p. 29). Thank you, Martha Stewart.

One year, my husband received a 24-pound turkey as a bonus from his company. I calculated that the bird would take about 8 hours to roast. Just after 6 a.m., I popped the pale, featherless carcass into the oven. But at about 1 p.m., the fire alarm started to beep. Smoke filled the kitchen. I opened the oven door and orange flames licked at the stove front. My husband doused the fire with the white foam from a trusty fire extinguisher.

We didn’t have turkey that day. We had hamburgers. I think my elderly grandmother actually preferred the Thanksgiving dinner that day.

This year, I will once again attempt to make my mother’s scalloped oysters. I will be the only one eating them, as my husband and daughter eschew eating shellfish. But that just means more for me.

I hope that I swerve closer to the perfect scalloped oysters of my memories, but even if I miss that mark, I know that I continue to honor a long-held family tradition.

We strive to taste the memories of the past, but tastes do change. Ingredients become hard to find and obsolete. And that’s absolutely okay.

Greene, M. P. (2009). Tips to cut down on holiday depression. New York Amsterdam News, 100(47), 26–27.

Sins, A. C. (2013). Doberge cake after Katrina. In Food matters: A Bedford spotlight reader (pp. 45–49). Bedford/St. Martin's.

#4637. BYD’s folding steering wheel isn’t a concept — it’s in a $49K SUV now

BYD launched a production SUV today with a steering wheel that folds flat into the dashboard. It comes standard on the top trim of the Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9, which sells for 329,900 yuan (about $49,000) in China.

Automakers and suppliers have been parading folding wheels on concept cars for about a decade. This is the first one customers can actually order, according to BYD.

The whole thing hinges on steer-by-wire. There’s no steering column physically connecting the wheel to the front wheels, so the wheel is just an input device, and BYD can put it wherever it wants.

On the Tai 9, it swings through 180 degrees on a hidden hinge and drops into a compartment in the dash in about 10 seconds. A panel closes over it, and a tray table folds out where the wheel used to be. Only the airbag remains outside of the compartment – keeping it useful with the steering wheel deployed or hidden.

It only folds when the vehicle is parked. Fang Cheng Bao pairs it with a driver’s seat that reclines to 165 degrees, so the pitch is simple: fold the wheel, lie back, and eat, nap, or play games while you charge or wait. The brand claims 80% of the driver’s area becomes usable space and rates the folding mechanism for 80,000 cycles.

When it’s deployed, it’s a regular D-shaped wheel with a full rim and physical buttons. No yoke. That’s a nice change from Tesla and Mercedes, which paired its new steer-by-wire system on the EQS with a yoke.

At the launch event, Fang Cheng Bao general manager Xiong Tianbo said the industry had been talking about folding steering wheels since 2016 without ever getting one into mass production. He added that BYD is using the same type of motor it develops for humanoid robots to move the wheel, a first in one of its cars.

Here’s Fang Cheng Bao’s official video of the feature:

China’s new national standard for steering systems took effect on July 1, 2026. It dropped the long-standing requirement for a mechanical link between the steering wheel and the road wheels, as long as the system meets redundancy and fail-safe rules.

Before that, steer-by-wire needed special approval. Nio’s ET9 was the first car in China to get it, back in December 2024. In the US, Tesla’s Cybertruck already uses it, and Mercedes is bringing it to the EQS this year.

Folding wheels themselves have stayed on show stands. BYD’s own Denza brand showed one on the Z concept at Shanghai in 2025. Autoliv and Tensor called theirs the “world’s first foldable steering wheel” at CES in January, for a Tensor Robocar they expected to reach volume production in the second half of 2026. Hyundai Mobis has been showing one for years.

Tesla went the other way with the Cybercab: no wheel at all. But the prototypes testing on public roads have a Cybertruck steering wheel bolted onto an exposed column, because a human still has to be able to drive.

The Tai 9 is Fang Cheng Bao’s biggest SUV yet. It’s 5,270 mm (207.5 in) long with a 3,130 mm wheelbase and six seats in a 2+2+2 layout. It’s also the first model on BYD’s new DMS hybrid platform.

A 1.5-liter turbo engine works with front and rear electric motors for a combined 400 kW (536 hp), and 0 to 100 km/h takes 4.8 seconds. The 66.48 kWh second-generation Blade battery supports BYD’s flash charging and delivers 310 km (193 miles) of electric range on the WLTC cycle. Rear-wheel steering, LiDAR, and BYD’s God’s Eye B driver assistance system are standard.

There are three trims: 279,900 yuan (about $41,700), 299,900 yuan, and 329,900 yuan. Only the top one gets the folding wheel.

Fang Cheng Bao sold 43,872 vehicles in October, up 41% year-over-year, mostly on the strength of the Tai 7. That model is now heading overseas: BYD sells it in the UK as the Ti 7. BYD hasn’t said anything about exporting the Tai 9.

It is not only that these technologies are impressive, but it is the speed at which they are being put into market by some of these Chinese car companies like BYD. They are moving further and further away from the competition but its understandable with the insane competition between car makers in China that they almost have to maintain and edge.

We’ve seen this at pretty much every auto show since the mid-2010s: a steering wheel slides away so the “driver” can relax while the car drives itself. It never shipped, for many reasons, but with steer-by-wire and autonomous driving now becoming reality, BYD is making the jump.

The Tai 9’s wheel only folds when you’re parked, so right now it’s a lounge feature. Recline the seat, stow the wheel, flip out the tray, and watch a movie while you charge. Is that a gimmick? A little. But Chinese EV buyers spend a lot of time in parked cars, and fridges, screens, and lie-flat seats sell cars there for a reason.

The bigger deal is underneath. The wheel can only fold because the Tai 9 is steer-by-wire, and BYD is putting that in a roughly $49,000 family SUV less than five months after China made it legal. After Cybertruck and now Mercedes with the EQS, we might be seeing the first steps of steer-by-wire actually becoming a more widely adopted technology.

#4636. Nearly 3 million pages of military records from the War of 1812 are finally online

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 2:01 PM EST

After 16 years of painstaking work, the National Archives and its collaborators have finally completed digitizing over 90,000 pension applications submitted to the United States government following the War of 1812. The project is more than just preservation for preservation’s sake. The roughly 2.8 million pages contain long-forgotten and missing details about 19th century Americans, their families, and their everyday lives.

While archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the new documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census. Patricia Oxley, president of the Federation of Genealogical Societies (FGS), explained the project was also incredibly time-sensitive.

“In the specific case of the War of 1812 pension records, there is an added priority due to their frail state where not acting may mean sacrificing these for future generations,” Oxley said in a recent announcement.

The somewhat new United States of America declared war on the United Kingdom on June 18, 1812, citing objections to trade restrictions with France amid the Napoleonic Wars, as well as the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors. Although the conflict famously included a British attack on Washington D.C. that resulted in the burning of the White House and U.S. Capitol, little shifted geopolitically between the two nations following the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent on February 17, 1815. The U.S. tallied around 15,000 casualties, while the U.K. and Canada saw about 10,700 deaths. Another 9,000 Indigenous fighters died while enlisted between the two sides.

Today’s military records are meticulously documented and stored digitally, but applying for benefits such as pensions was a much more labor-intensive process during the 19th century. With the burden of proof on each applicant, veterans were required to supply lengthy accounts of their service. Each War of 1812 pension file is liable to contain not just combat information, but the names and personal details of fellow soldiers, family members, spouses, and countless other relations.

“Our users have been asking for the War of 1812 pension records for some time, and I expect this collection to be very popular based on the rich war time detail it contains,” added Brian Hansen, general manager at Fold3, Ancestry’s military records service and National Archives collaborator.

The collection also includes a full-text search feature using handwriting recognition technology. This lets users explore the files based on every named individual, and not simply the primary veteran applicants. The pension records are currently available for free on Fold3’s website, and are being added to the National Archives catalog on a rolling basis.

Correction 11/20/26 9:30 a.m. EST: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated the pension archive contained around 7 million files. This was based on an initial assessment from researchers in 2010. The article has been updated to reflect the more accurate tally.

#4635. Hyundai claims 2027’s ‘Best EV Brand’ title as the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 impress

Hyundai’s electric SUVs are getting some love. The IONIQ 5 and three-row IONIQ 9 helped the Korean automaker land its first-ever “Best Electric Vehicle Brand” award from US News & World Report for 2027.

“This win showcases the breadth and strength of Hyundai’s SUV and electric lineups,” Alex Kwanten, managing editor at Autos at US News, said after naming it the Best EV Brand and Best SUV Brand for 2027.

This marks the first time Hyundai has earned the Best EV Brand award and the third consecutive win for Best SUV Brand.

Including hybrid and electric vehicles, Hyundai offers ten unique SUVs, “many of them at or near the top of our rankings in those classes for capability, comfort, performance and value,” Kwanten said.

Hyundai’s fully electric SUVs, the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9, “in particular, stand out for their combination of style and technology,” he explained.

Hyundai currently offers the IONIQ 5, including the sporty IONIQ 5 N and off-road-focused IONIQ 5 XRT, plus the three-row IONIQ 9.

Although Hyundai discontinued its electric sedan, the IONIQ 6, after the 2025 model year, the new high-performance IONIQ 6 N joins the lineup in 2027.

The IONIQ 5 continued to earn praise, taking its third consecutive Best Compact Electric SUV award. Its larger sibling, the IONIQ 9, took the top spot in the midsize electric SUV category.

Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in the US this year through September that isn’t a Tesla, ranking third behind the Model Y and Model 3.

Why does it continue winning over buyers? The IONIQ 5 checks all the boxes with long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior with modern tech.

It’s also among the most affordable EVs in the US. Prices for the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 start at just $35,250.

However, the base price is for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model costs an extra $2,500, with prices starting at $37,750, but it offers up to 318 miles of range.

The three-row Hyundai IONIQ 9 electric SUV starts at $58,955 with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles.

Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is about the size of a Tesla Model Y, with two rows of seating and space for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating with six- or seven-seat options.

The larger IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with up to 106.5 cubic feet in the IONIQ 5.

Both electric SUVs use an 800-volt electrical architecture for ultra-fast charging. The IONIQ 5 can charge from 10% to 80% in about 20 minutes, while the IONIQ 9 takes around 24 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Hyundai assembles the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

Turn off reality TV and turn on the bald eagle cams. It’s all the drama you need.

When internet-famous bald eagle Shadow seemingly welcomed a mysterious new female into his nest earlier this week, many fans have questioned the whereabouts of Kaydee. After the death of Shadow’s longtime partner Jackie in August, he had been spotted spending time with the 4-year-old banded female eagle named KD1 (later renamed Kaydee). It seemed like the eagles might head into mating season as a pair, but after the arrival of a new, large female, it’s unclear how the relationships will all shake out.

Since the appearance of the mystery female, nicknamed Big Beautiful Visitor or BBV by some fans, Kaydee has disappeared from view of Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV)’s two cameras. She was last spotted by the cameras on November 14 in the Roost Tree, according to FOBBV. Despite concerns that she may be injured or had left the area, wildlife photographers have continued to document Kaydee’s presence near Big Bear Lake as recently as November 18.

Photographer Alla Shumko shared photos of Kaydee perched near Big Bear Lake on November 18. Kaydee’s double bands are visible as she observed a scuffle between younger eagles fighting over fish.

Mating season is well underway, so viewers of FOBBV’s 24/7 livecams have been watching closely for signs that Shadow has selected a new partner. Shadow has worked with both Kaydee and the new eagle on nest maintenance and shared “beaky kisses” with each female, both signs of bonding in bald eagles. Bald eagle mating involves a bit of aerial acrobatics—copulating pairs can be seen in what’s called a “cartwheel display,” in which they lock talons in mid-air while tumbling down to the ground. Male eagles do not have an external phallus, so mating occurs via a touch of cloacas. Vocalizations can typically be heard during the act, which lasts about 7 to 12 seconds, according to Raptor Resource.

As this is nature, we humans can’t predict or influence who Shadow will pick as a new partner. Or if he picks at all. All we can do is watch and wait and let nature take its course.

#4633. Conformity, Individuality, and the Lawns of Levittown

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Just a few miles from my home is historic Levittown, Long Island, where immediately after WWII, 4,000 acres of potato fields were plowed under to mass-produce more than 17,000 detached houses; many of these four-and-a-half-room homes were constructed in about two days.

Selling for less than $8,000 ($115,000 in 2024 dollars), each house came with a TV set and hi-fi. Buyers could choose a red, yellow, or blue house in one of three styles, in neighborhoods largely devoid of trees. This first modern suburb prompted historian Lewis Mumford to describe Levittown as “a uniform environment from which escape is impossible.”

A popular folksong tagged Levittown and other such developments as places of little boxes “made out of ticky tacky/And they all look the same.” No longer.

Drive through the area today, and it is nearly impossible to imagine the architectural conformity that it once was. What is striking about Levittown is that as houses aged, they became distinctive from one another and went decidedly upscale. They expanded upward and sideways. These four-and-a-half-room homes now are four- or five-bedroom houses with two baths. Barren landscapes are long gone. In 2024, Levittown houses were listed in the $700,000 range.

The sterile 1950s transformed into the turbulent '60s, with subsequent decades bringing tremendous social change in their wake. New generations moved in with new ideas; they had more money than did the returning war veterans. With time, Levittown’s appearance reflected the tastes of new homeowners.

Levittown reflects two contradictory impulses in human nature: The individuality impulse on the one hand, and conformity on the other. It is the universal desire to be recognized as a unique individual but at the same time desiring to be part of a group. The distinctiveness of the home displays this while adhering to the idealized standard of a suburban front lawn. You can drive for miles through Levittown—and almost every suburban neighborhood—and find that while the houses are no longer alike, not a single house has dispensed with grass lawns.

This would be a landscaping choice if it didn’t also mean that, to maintain the carpet-like appearance, the air is polluted with the fumes of mowers, the groundwater is poisoned with fertilizers (Long Island depends exclusively on its aquifer for its drinking water), and a din created by leaf blowers makes a quiet summer day around the house a rare event. Dispensing with lawns will probably have to be a policy decision, as there is only so much individuality that a person can express without feeling like an outsider. The change will have to come as an imposed municipal edict; not having a manicured lawn becomes a new enforced norm, where conformity becomes not having a grassy lawn.

#4631. North Atlantic right whales named after Dolly Parton and Gonzo

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Less than 400 adult North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) still exist in the wild, making them one of the world’s most critically endangered species. Of those, 20 have officially received spiffy new names from conservationists at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life. The researchers curate the annual North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog, and attach personable monikers to a select few baleen cetaceans in order to more easily monitor them. This year, it’s time to wave hello to Dodo, Volcano, and Dolly.

“Naming right whales is a fun and creative activity for our research community, but it also allows an opportunity to connect with the whales on an individual level,” Amy Warren, an aquarium scientific program officer and name project coordinator, said in Anderson Cabot Center’s announcement. “It can be hard to relate to Catalog #5299, but a whale named Nibbles is bound to be memorable.”

The 2026 inductees also include Grand Slam (Catalog #3991) and Slide (Catalog #4991). The sister whales have a mother named Fenway (Catalog #2791), who was also named in honor of the Boston Red Sox. Grand Slam earned her new name thanks to her three patches of raised tissue known as callosities that resemble the bases on a baseball field. Meanwhile, Slide received their name due to the curved scar on her back that recalls someone sliding through home plate. Other right whale names this year include Goose, Donegal, and even Gonzo for the beloved Muppet.

“Although the names are intended to help researchers at sea, they also give the general public a better understanding of the individual whales,” added Caroline Mowdy, a spokesperson for Whale and Dolphin Conservation (WDC).

Collaborators at the WDC also created some lighthearted, yearbook-esque biographies for each whale. For example, Dolly (Catalog #4191), whose callosity looks strikingly similar to the late, great country singer’s larger-than-life hair, apparently loves the song, “Jolene.” Then again, who doesn’t?

“We see these whales and their families grow each year,” said Mowdy. “Knowing them makes the tragedies even more tragic, but it also makes our determination to protect them even stronger.”

On Monday, the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium announced that there are roughly 382 North Atlantic right whales, representing a 1.8 percent drop in population size from the 2024 estimate. Their primary threats remain getting tangled in fishing line and vessel strikes.

However, even amid their struggles, the 2025–2026 right whale calving season saw the most calves born since 2009. A total of 24 calves were born, including a surprising late addition that was spotted in Canada in September.

Kia’s EV lineup covers just about every size and price point, but it believes one thing is still missing: a truly cheap electric car. That’s about to change in 2027, when Kia plans to unveil a new EV that could start at around $22,000 to $24,000.

It’s been 40 years since Kia introduced its first electric vehicle, the Besta EV, created so runners in the 1986 Asian Games wouldn’t have to breathe toxic fumes from the broadcast vehicle.

Kia has come a long way since the Besta EV hit the road, now offering a complete lineup of electric vehicles, from compact SUVs and hatchbacks to vans and three-row SUVs.

In Europe and the UK, Kia’s electric lineup consists of the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van, but the Korean automaker isn’t done yet.

“With no intention of resting on its laurels,” Kia said, the brand plans to complete development of its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) by the end of 2027, an all-new B-segment EV hatchback.

It didn’t offer any other details on the upcoming EV, but Ted Lee, Kia’s executive vice president and head of global operations, told Auto Express that Kia and Hyundai are co-developing a new dedicated EV architecture for an upcoming pair of entry-level electric cars.

Expected to arrive as the Hyundai IONIQ 1 and Kia EV1, the new EVs will compete with other entry-level electric cars like the Renault Twingo, which starts at about €20,000.

Lee said the EV1’s price will be highly competitive not just with other entry-level EVs, but also with small gas-powered cars, with prices expected to start in the €20,000 to €22,000 range, or about $22,000 to $24,000. And that’s without government incentives.

The EV2 starts at just €26,600 ($29,500) in Germany and other European markets as Kia’s current entry-level EV, so the price range would make sense.

While it will be Kia’s cheapest EV, Lee promised it would not cut corners in quality, design, or features.

As its first SDV, the EV1 will feature Kia and Hyundai Motor’s latest-generation tech and software. Kia said the electric SDV will offer Level 2+ autonomous driving on highways. In 2029, Kia plans to expand to Level 2++, enabling it to operate in cities.

The new EV will also use Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), the Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.

What will the EV1 look like? According to Auto Express, the entry-level EV will look a bit sportier and less boxy than the EV2 SUV. It could draw inspiration from the Vision Meta Turismo concept.

It also apparently won’t be based on the Picanto, Kia’s smallest gas-powered car. The Kia EV1 is expected to bring a unique style to the family.

This is good to see and makes sense, especially in Europe. I don't think Kia can go wrong making vehicles at so many different price points. It allows them to reach different segments and almost literally have something for almost everyone.

While all of Kia’s current EVs feature its ccNC infotainment system with dual 12.3″ instrument display and infotainment screens, plus a 5″ climate control panel, the EV1 could bring a simpler setup.

Like its other electric models, the EV1 is expected to receive the GT treatment. However, as an entry-level model, it may not use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup like the others.

Will Kia bring the EV1 to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. Kia has previously said the B-segment hatchback is designed for Europe. It could even be built alongside the EV2 at Kia’s plant in Slovakia.

The good news? The EV3, Kia’s compact electric SUV, is now on sale in the US, starting at just $29,890.

#4629. The Failure Rate of Public Schools Is a Tragedy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

As described in the article “In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?,” teenager Najya Hannah-Jones confronted her mother, the prominent journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, about the choice to send her to public school in a system that, for many, provides substandard education. It was refreshing to read of Najya fighting to get a better education, a striking contrast with the popular but often inaccurate stereotype of lazy teens aiming to learn as little as possible. More importantly, kudos to Nikole Hannah-Jones for candidly admitting in her article that teachers lied to her about what they were teaching and, worse, tried to deceive both mother and daughter about what had actually been learned.

Every parent has a duty to nurture their children, but all parents also must consider their values when choosing schools for their children, so it is heartbreaking to realize that Ms. Hannah-Jones could have chosen a far better public school in New York for her daughter that would have met the core values listed in her article. Public school? Check. Racially diverse or perhaps even predominately Black student body? Check. Most importantly, a track record of meeting educational standards and being honest with parents regarding what their child is learning and how they are performing? Check and check.

The truth is that Nikole Hannah-Jones could have enrolled her daughter in a local public school where the majority of students are Black and other nonwhite families and has long offered much better odds for positive educational outcomes. There has long been such an option available to parents that is too often ignored: New York City charter schools.

In the book Charter Schools and Their Enemies, Thomas Sowell painstakingly and convincingly shows that public charter schools in New York City consistently outperform neighborhood schools. Based on Ms. Hannah-Jones essay, one could argue that is not an especially high bar, but the data in the book show academic superiority relative to even the higher-quality schools in New York City, New York State, and nationwide. It is noteworthy that Sowell meticulously controls for the usual “straw men” used to assault charter schools. Indeed, some of the charter schools were not only in the same neighborhoods, but in the same building as the comparison schools in his study.

It is an ongoing tragedy that Ms. Hannah-Jones and others in the Black community are not demanding an expansion of public charter school options for their children. After all, and perhaps this is why they are under assault, public charter schools provide prima facia evidence that New York can, in fact, deliver a high-quality public education, but chooses not to do so. One hopes that other families like the Hannah-Joneses will enroll their children in public charter schools and demand that New York City be more honest what is being taught and what their children have learned.

The national discussion Ms. Hannah-Jones has sparked has been overwhelmingly focused on schools with majority Black student enrollment, but the debate should not be narrowly circumscribed. The truth is that every teen enrolled in failing schools across the U.S. should be asking their parents the same question Najya Hannah-Jones asked her mother: Why are you sending me to a school you already know is delivering a substandard education?

Stripped to essentials, Ms. Hannah-Jones faced the same choice most families do when deciding whether to enroll their children in public schools, regardless of race: If I send my child to the local school as a kindergartner, what is the probability that my child will emerge from 8th grade with the basic reading and math skills needed to succeed in high school and beyond? It turns out that there are ample data to help parents answer this question.

The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) provides annual statistics on U.S. education outcomes. Nationally, only 26% of 8th-graders are proficient or above in math, according to its 2022 Nation's Report Card; only about one in four children are entering high school with grade-level proficiency in math. Reading outcomes are only slightly better, with 28% of 8th-graders being rated as proficient. Candidly, this is a national disgrace that poses an excruciating dilemma for parents and students.

A usual response to this data is to argue that public schools are underfunded. New York spends an average of more than $30,000 per student. Overall, the U.S. consistently spends more per pupil than nearly every other country in the world, including many that deliver better outcomes while paying less than half of what the U.S spends. More money is not translating to better outcomes. Does anyone believe that even doubling expenditures or even tripling them would appreciably improve outcomes at the school Najya Hannah-Jones attended, or any other failing school? After all, real spending, even adjusted for inflation, has more than doubled in the past 25 years and outcomes are actually a bit worse nationwide over the same period.

If it is not simply spending more money, what should parents do? The best answer: Do your homework. There are often options. Many states have adopted public options, including public charter schools, public magnet schools, and other similar approaches.

Several of my own children attended a public school implementing a Montessori teaching approach and two of my granddaughters are currently enrolled in a similar public school in Nashville. I was (and am) very pleased with what they were taught, how they were taught, and what they learned. Another daughter attended an academic magnet public high school that consistently outperforms even the most expensive private schools, even though, in general, Nashville public schools often have relatively poor outcomes for most students. The evidence is overwhelming that public school systems know how to deliver a high-quality education. Why are they choosing not to? Najya Hannah-Jones is absolutely right to demand answers and all teens—and their parents—should be asking the same questions.

Sowell, T. (2020). Charter schools and their enemies. Basic Books.

#4628. New electric comb from China regrew nearly 100% of hair (in mice)

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 4:10 PM EST

A potentially revolutionary electronic comb is generating some pretty hair-raising results. The experimental comb has been used to successfully restore nearly all the hair in bald test subjects. But don’t chuck out that Rogaine just yet. The comb’s users were mice with shaved backs.

Though the Detangle comb (named after the 2010 Disney film Tangled) hasn’t been tested on humans yet, the Chinese scientist behind its development says the eye-grabbing results on our distant genetic cousins suggest it could play a role in the neverending quest to keep those luscious locks just a hair longer.

Created by a team led by Beihang University in Beijing, the comb initially looks like the chunky plastic kind adorning typical pharmacy aisles. However, a closer look at its clear plastic handle reveals a green circuit board. Further down, one can see electrodes embedded in the comb’s teeth, which alternate between long and short. The team says that this height variance makes the comb’s pulsed electric field more than two and a half times stronger than it would be with evenly matched teeth.

The shorter teeth also contain two experimental genetic treatments. One boosts blood vessel growth around the hair follicles. The other treatment  blocks dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone known to shrink follicles. The electric field generated by the comb temporarily opens up skin so the treatments can get inside, reaching up to nine times deeper into the follicle region than a conventional cream.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Researchers performed a variety of tests on mice that had their backs shaved and were given testosterone to mimic pattern baldness. Over 28 days, the balding mice were treated with minoxidil or finasteride (the current standards for medical hair restoration), the comb’s electrical stimulation alone, and the comb combined with an experimental genetic treatment. Mice given finasteride regrew about 50 percent of their hair, while the ones on and minoxidil regrew 70 percent. Those numbers  honestly aren’t  too bad on their own, but the results were even better when Detangle got involved. Mice treated with the comb and both experimental treatments saw a staggering 97.85 percent hair regrowth. And all without having to book a flight to Turkey for a hair transplant.

“[T]hese results demonstrate that electrostimulation via the Detangle system promotes hair growth and follicle regeneration in a safe and effective manner,” the team wrote in their paper published earlier this month in the Nature Communications.

The potential market for a hair regrowing comb is sizable to say the least. Detangle’’s creators say androgenetic alopecia, the scientific term for pattern baldness, affects 1.5 billion people worldwide. Some studies suggest up to 80 percent of men will experience pattern baldness, with  some populations seeing symptoms before the age of 40. Somewhere between one fifth and two fifths of women may also experience pattern hair thinning. And hair isn’t just hair. Social expectations and norms around hair partly explain why hair loss can carry psychological baggage.

Scientists and hair care providers know this, of course. Toupees, tonics, and tinctures promising to reverse nature’s balding date back thousands of years. Today, the standard medical treatment usually involves topical minoxidil (the active ingredient in Rogaine) and oral finasteride. Minoxidil generally works, but results vary widely from person to person and it requires constant, ongoing application.

Finasteride is often far more effective, with long-term studies showing it can preserve hair in most men for at least a decade, but it also carries the risk for much more intense side effects. The drug (which saw a surge in popularity thanks to online, telehealth services) has been linked to decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. Some patients have also reported anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts. While the side effects are uncommon, the risk presented a potentially steep trade off for a fuller head of hair.

Those intrigued by the comb will unfortunately have to hold out quite a bit longer. The team says more research is needed before the device is tested on humans and, even then, there’s no guarantee the rodent results will translate. Testosterone-induced hair loss on a shaved mouse back is a far cry from human pattern baldness, which typically creeps in over years.

It’s also worth emphasizing that the electric comb, memorable as it is, wasn’t solely responsible for the best results. The pair of experimental genetic treatments used in the study (called SRD5A2 siRNA and VEGFA plasmids) also need to be tested in humans to ensure they are safe and don’t come with unintended side effects of their own. Wig stores, it seems, will live to see another day.

Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore. She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many.”

Last week, a child’s knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remained stuck in her digestive track. She had undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that showed intestinal bunching, indicating her body was trying and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests. Just yesterday, on November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers.

“Fiona was such a gift,” said Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”

#4626. Every Choice Is a Loss: Why We Often Regret Lives Not Lived

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Nurses often recount stories of patients near the end of their lives who express regrets about experiences they never had and paths they never took. They sometimes wonder whether choosing differently might have made them more satisfied with their lives. Regret is, to some extent, part of almost everyone's life. If we marry, we may eventually regret it; if we do not, we may remain alone and regret that too. If we emigrate, we may regret leaving; if we stay and endure our circumstances, we may regret that as well. Whether we remain in a tedious job or choose another, whether we speak our minds to those around us or keep silent, we may still end up regretting our choices.

In the first part of Either/Or, Søren Kierkegaard—writing through the persona of a young man, "A"—posits that life is inherently characterized by boredom and that the choices we make are attempts to escape this state. We choose things that promise pleasure, yet such choices never lead to lasting joy or satisfaction; what is thrilling today may become mundane and tedious by tomorrow. Boredom inevitably returns, leaving us to lament the choices we made and wish we had chosen differently. To break this cycle of regret and boredom, "A" offers an intriguing proposal: much like farmers who rotate crops to prevent soil erosion, individuals should constantly alter their approach to life—avoiding fixation on any single experience—in order to mitigate boredom. Praising the character of Don Juan—the seductive, womanizing figure from Mozart’s opera—"A" champions the rejection of all commitments as a means to banish boredom and regret. In the same volume, Kierkegaard introduces another character, Johannes, who employs psychological tactics to seduce a young woman named Cordelia, gradually cultivating her affection. He uses strategies such as maintaining distance, employing silence, sowing doubt, and stirring the other person’s emotions—all of which he finds deeply pleasurable.

In the second part, Kierkegaard writes through another persona, Judge Wilhelm. He recommends that “A” choose an ethical and committed life. A significant portion of this section addresses marriage. Wilhelm argues that only a stable, committed relationship can prevent the initial fire of love and passion from quickly burning out, allowing it instead to endure. Through Wilhelm's voice, Kierkegaard writes that our choices shape our ultimate selves—an idea later further developed within existentialist philosophy. By employing pseudonymous characters, Kierkegaard deliberately avoids taking sides, leaving the conclusion to the reader. Ultimately, he presents choice and regret as fundamental components of human existence [1].

Now, we explore the neurological mechanisms underlying the persistent human experience of regret. In their book The Molecule of More, Lieberman and Long discuss two brain circuits—the mesolimbic and the mesocortical—both of which utilize dopamine as a neurotransmitter. The first circuit primarily drives "wanting," motivation, and the anticipation of a reward; it is not about the pleasure itself but rather the anticipated pleasure expected from a given stimulus. The second circuit activates top-down pathways for impulse control, enabling consideration of the future consequences of one's decisions and desires. From an evolutionary perspective, this capacity has allowed humans to transcend immediate, relatively simple responses and plan for the attainment of long-term goals. However, this simplified model of the reward system’s neurology suggests that repetition of a stimulus leads to a diminished reward—driven by a decline in dopamine levels and function within the mesolimbic system—thereby shifting attention and motivation toward new rewards [2].

Although the prefrontal cortex is primarily responsible for logical reasoning, evaluation, and behavioral regulation, certain regions within it also play a role in generating feelings of regret. A 2004 study revealed that individuals with damage to the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), unlike healthy controls, did not report experiencing regret or anticipating negative outcomes during a gambling task. Additionally, other brain areas, such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the hippocampus, contribute to the experience of regret by enabling the mental simulation of alternative, unlived scenarios [3].

In an intriguing paper published in Science Advances in 2023, researchers examined the distinct roles of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the ventral striatum, and dopaminergic neurons in counterfactual thinking in monkeys. Their findings indicated that the brain can represent not only the reward actually received but also the value of a reward that could have been obtained through a different choice [4]. This suggests that, at times, the source of our regret is not an event that actually occurred in real life, but rather an event that never took place, yet one whose possibility the mind has retained. In effect, we may find ourselves mourning a life we ​​never lived.

In conclusion, the human brain is designed to anticipate the future outcomes of decisions we might have made and to compare those potential results with our current situation. While this capacity can aid in making better future choices, it can also foster a chronic sense of regret. This trait leads us to constantly evaluate our present circumstances against hypothetical alternatives—lamenting the paths we did not take. In the modern era, this inclination has been exacerbated by the rise of social media, which offers numerous opportunities for social comparison and exposes us to constant reminders of "alternative" lives. Observing the lives, homes, cities, and joys of others can trigger anxiety that we are perpetually falling behind.

Here, it helps to distinguish this phenomenon into two types: 1) Constructive Regret, which helps us recognize past mistakes and make better decisions moving forward; and 2) Ruminative Regret, which traps individuals in a cycle of constantly comparing their actual lives with hypothetical scenarios or the lives of others—without necessarily leading to any constructive action or decision. Since it is impossible to experience every life possibility or to know for certain whether a different choice would have been better, we can take the message of the second part of Either/Or to heart: By committing fully to our own lives, rather than constantly dwelling on lost possibilities, we can liberate ourselves from the anxiety and the wearying melancholy of regret.

1. Kierkegaard, S., Hannay, A., & Eremita, V. (2004). Either/Or: A Fragment of Life. Penguin Books Limited.

2. Lieberman, D. Z. and M. E. Long (2018). The Molecule of More: How a Single Chemical in Your Brain Drives Love, Sex, and Creativity--and Will Determine the Fate of the Human Race, BenBella Books.

3. Camille N, Coricelli G, Sallet J, Pradat-Diehl P, Duhamel JR, Sirigu A. The involvement of the orbitofrontal cortex in the experience of regret. Science. 2004 May 21;304(5674):1167-70.

4. Yun M, Nejime M, Kawai T, Kunimatsu J, Yamada H, Kim HR, Matsumoto M. Distinct roles of the orbitofrontal cortex, ventral striatum, and dopamine neurons in counterfactual thinking of decision outcomes. Sci Adv. 2023 Aug 9;9(32):eadh2831.
